articles.title: The microbiota-drug delivery nexus: from pharmacomicrobiomics to live biotherapeutic delivery.
articles.abstract: The human microbiota, being the diverse communities of bacteria, archaea, fungi, and viruses colonising the gut, skin, respiratory tract, and urogenital system is now recognised as a critical, yet frequently overlooked, determinant of pharmaceutical outcomes. The emerging field of pharmacomicrobiomics has established that microbiota compositional and functional variation profoundly influences drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and toxicity, whilst drugs reciprocally reshape microbial community structure. However, a fundamental dimension of this relationship has received insufficient attention: the drug delivery system itself is not a passive vehicle but an active participant in microbiota-drug interactions. The physicochemical properties of delivery vehicles, the excipients they contain, and the pharmacokinetic profiles they impose each alter the nature, site, and duration of drug-microbe contact in ways that have significant consequences for therapeutic outcomes. Conversely, the microbiota modulates the performance of drug delivery systems through degrading carriers, altering mucosal permeability, and modifying the environment in which release occurs. Beyond these bidirectional interactions, controlled release technology offers a distinct and compelling opportunity, including the deliberate exploitation of microbial metabolic activity as a trigger for site-specific drug release and the delivery of the microbiota itself. This review introduces the concept of the microbiota-drug delivery nexus, providing the first comprehensive account of the bidirectional interactions between drug delivery systems and the human microbiota, with a specific focus on how oral and non-oral delivery vehicles interact with the gut microbiota. Critical knowledge gaps are identified, which highlight emerging opportunities for microbiota-informed formulation design, and make the case that incorporating microbiota considerations into drug delivery science is no longer optional but essential for the rational development of next-generation therapeutics.

articles.title: Neuropathy target esterase-associated delayed neurotoxicity: a silent threat in organophosphorus poisoning.
articles.abstract: Neuropathy target esterase (NTE), localized predominantly to the endoplasmic reticulum, is highly expressed within the nervous system. Under physiological conditions, NTE functions mainly as a phospholipase B/lysophospholipase involved in phosphatidylcholine and lysophosphatidylcholine turnover, thereby maintaining phospholipid homeostasis, membrane integrity, and axonal stability. In toxicology, NTE is of particular interest as the principal molecular target in organophosphorus-induced delayed neurotoxicity (OPIDN), a syndrome that develops days to weeks after exposure to certain organophosphorus (OP) compounds. Unlike acute cholinergic toxicity caused by acetylcholinesterase inhibition, OPIDN is initiated by inhibition of NTE followed by "aging" of the enzyme-inhibitor complex, an essentially irreversible process considered critical for neuropathic outcome. The resulting loss of NTE activity disrupts phospholipid metabolism, promotes lysophospholipid accumulation, endoplasmic reticulum stress, calcium dyshomeostasis, and cytoskeletal breakdown, leading to distal axon degeneration in both the central and peripheral nervous systems. Clinically, OPIDN manifests after a latent phase with progressive weakness, sensory abnormalities, gait impairment, and in severe cases persistent spasticity or paralysis. This review summarizes the current knowledge on NTE structure, catalytic function, tissue distribution, and physiological significance, and integrates these findings with the molecular and clinical features of OPIDN. Particular attention is paid to the distinction between aging (neuropathic) and non-aging (non-neuropathic) NTE inhibitors, the structural determinants of neuropathic potential, and its clinical implications.

articles.title: Mechanistic pathways of cosmetic ingredient toxicity: a critical review of in vitro and in vivo evidence.
articles.abstract: Every day, billions of people apply cosmetic products containing dozens of bioactive compounds whose combined toxicological profile has never been formally evaluated. Human biomonitoring confirms systemic deposition of these compounds in blood, adipose tissue, placenta, and breast milk worldwide. This scoping review, following PRISMA-ScR, synthesizes in vitro and in vivo mechanistic toxicology evidence for six major cosmetic ingredient categories-preservatives, UV filters, engineered nanoparticles, fragrances, surfactants, and colorants-and maps findings onto established adverse outcome pathways (AOPs). Searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science identified 1231 records, of which 48 studies met eligibility criteria. Critical appraisal exposes three structural failures: most studies test at concentrations orders of magnitude above realistic dermal exposures; nearly all assess single ingredients in isolation; and the field over-relies on targeted assays over untargeted omics. The evidence nonetheless reveals mechanistic convergence: parabens, benzophenones, UV filters, and surfactants activate overlapping estrogen receptor, oxidative stress, and innate immune pathways, with biological plausibility supported by cohort data linking benzophenone-3 to lower testosterone and altered pubertal timing, and the preservatives chloromethylisothiazolinone/methylisothiazolinone to Th2-skewed atopic responses. AOP mapping shows uneven regulatory readiness: skin sensitization (AOP40) is the most mature pathway; estrogen and androgen receptor activity (AOP29, AOP19) and thyroid disruption (AOP54) are existing anchors needing refinement; and three candidate AOPs are proposed. We propose a four-tier, largely non-animal integrated testing strategy compatible with EU Regulation 1223/2009 and the US Modernization of Cosmetics Regulation Act of 2022, alongside six priority research gaps to guide future regulatory risk assessment of cosmetic ingredients.

articles.title: Epigenetic markers as predictors of neurotoxicity and abuse potential of psychotropic drugs: integration of epigenetic modifications in New Approach Methodologies.
articles.abstract: Neurotoxicity and abuse potential are strongly associated with psychotropic drugs. Although animal models have been used for decades to investigate different forms of toxicity, including neurotoxicity and abuse potential, increasing efforts have been directed toward overcoming their inherent limitations. In this context, the development of New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), aimed at improving chemical safety assessment through more protective and physiologically relevant models, has emerged as a promising strategy to predict the neurotoxic potential of drugs while contributing to the replacement, reduction, and refinement of animal experimentation. Nevertheless, the number of NAMs capable of reliably and efficiently predicting neurotoxicity remains limited. Importantly, psychotropic drugs have been shown to induce epigenetic modifications (e.g., DNA methylation, histone modifications), which are frequently associated with neurotoxic adverse effects. The integration of these alterations into NAMs may therefore represent a major advance for academia, industry, and regulatory agencies in assessing the neurotoxic and abuse potential of such substances. Here, we review the latest evidence on the role of psychotropic drug-induced epigenetic modifications in neurotoxicity and abuse potential. Importantly, we further discuss how integrating these epigenetic alterations into NAMs could advance risk assessment of neurotoxic effects and abuse liability.

articles.title: Hormesis as a universal cellular strategy for growth.
articles.abstract: Our review synthesizes a vast and dispersed literature to demonstrate that subtoxic doses of structurally diverse chemicals can induce a conserved growth-stimulatory (hormetic) response across bacterial, microalgal, plant, and mammalian cells. Stimulation is concentration- and exposure-time-dependent, with higher concentrations inhibiting growth. In eukaryotic models, moderate ROS signaling and activation of DNA-PKcs/Akt, ERK1/2, PI3K/AKT, mTOR, or AURKA accompany growth stimulation, with Cyclin D-CDK4 promoting G1/S transition in mammalian cells. The proliferative DNA-PKcs/Akt response is observed in human hepatic cells, while bacterial examples involve LuxR-dependent signaling and fatty acid β-oxidation. Metabolism rewires, with some microalgae enhancing glycolysis and Krebs cycling, whereas other photosynthetic microorganisms reroute photosynthetic carbon toward lipid or starch storage while downregulating selected carbohydrate-catabolic proteins. Nrf2-driven antioxidants in mammalian cells, carotenoids, and detoxifying enzymes are upregulated, establishing a preconditioned state that can attenuate apoptosis upon subsequent challenge. Within the Catabolic-Anabolic Cycling Hormesis (CACH) model, some time-dependent responses are consistent with an anabolic overshoot following a transient catabolic decline (ATP depletion). This anabolic reprogramming accompanies biofilm formation, altered motility, and, in neoplastic cells, anchorage-independent growth. Thus, cell proliferation is a metabolic strategy shaped by adversity, with functional consequences that depend on cellular context and the endpoint assessed.

articles.title: From TD50 to benchmark dose in nitrosamine risk assessment: evidence from N-Nitrosotrimetazidine carcinogenicity and TGR mutation data.
articles.abstract: The presence of N-nitrosamine drug substance-related impurities (NDSRIs) in pharmaceuticals represents a significant regulatory and safety challenge due to their classification as a "cohort of concern." This paper describes the toxicological evaluation of N-Nitrosotrimetazidine (NTMZ), performed to refine the initial default acceptable intake (AI) limits of 18-26.5 ng/day and the later published value of 400 ng/day, established using the Carcinogenic Potency Categorization Approach (CPCA). The evaluation followed a tiered approach: NTMZ was first confirmed as mutagenic in vitro in a standard Ames test. To further investigate its genotoxic potential, two in vivo studies were conducted in Wistar and transgenic rats. DNA strand breaks in the liver and duodenum (comet assay) and positive results in the Transgenic Rodent (TGR) confirmed an in vivo mutagenic mode of action. Benchmark Dose (BMD) analysis of the TGR data yielded a BMDL50 of 7 mg/kg/day in male rat livers. To characterize long-term carcinogenic risk, a GLP-compliant 2-year carcinogenicity study was conducted in Wistar rats. Chronic exposure induced liver (hemangiosarcomas, hepatocellular carcinomas and adenomas) and intestinal tumors (adenomas and adenocarcinomas), leading to a Tumor Dose 50 (TD50) of 23 mg/kg/day in male rats. BMD analysis of tumor incidence identified the lowest BMDL10 of 2.6 mg/kg/day in females, used to derive an AI of 13 µg/day. Strong concordance between the transgenic rat BMD, carcinogenicity-study BMDL10 and TD50 supported derivation of a conservative AI of 13 µg/person/day based on the BMDL10 and further support regulatory acceptance and use of BMD-derived approaches for nitrosamine evaluation.

articles.title: Mechanistic insights into PFAS-induced toxicity: from lipid membrane perturbation to ion channel and transporter dysregulation.
articles.abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental contaminants associated with a wide range of adverse health outcomes, including metabolic, developmental, and neurodevelopmental disorders. Recent evidence suggests that PFAS can act as membrane-active compounds, directly interacting with lipid bilayers. Their amphiphilic properties allow incorporation into cellular membranes, altering membrane properties. These physicochemical changes can impact the structural dynamics and functional properties of membrane proteins, particularly ion channels. A growing body of research demonstrates that PFAS modulate the activity of multiple ion channel types, including voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels, glutamate receptors, GABAA receptors, and K⁺ channels, as well as intracellular channels such as ryanodine receptors, voltage-dependent anion channels (VDACs), and mitochondrial calcium uniporters. These effects are often observed as shifts in channel gating, conductance, and voltage dependence rather than as competition at defined ligand-binding sites, a pattern compatible with membrane perturbation acting as one contributing influence alongside direct protein interactions and other lipid-mediated mechanisms. PFAS also interact with plasma membrane transporters, altering the transport of endogenous substrates while utilizing transport systems such as organic anion and bile acid transporters for their own cellular uptake, tissue distribution, and elimination. Thus, membrane transport proteins may function both as targets of PFAS toxicity and as determinants of PFAS disposition. These effects extend beyond the plasma membrane to intracellular organelles. PFAS have been associated with Ca²⁺ and iron homeostasis across the endoplasmic reticulum-mitochondrial axis, promoting mitochondrial dysfunction, reactive oxygen species generation, and activation of cell death pathways. These observations suggest that ion channel dysfunction may contribute to the link membrane perturbations to downstream cellular damage. This review integrates current evidence on PFAS-induced membrane perturbation and ion channel dysregulation and situates these mechanisms within a multiscale framework encompassing membrane biophysics, organelle signaling, and cellular toxicity. This perspective offers a mechanistic framework for PFAS toxicity and underscores the need for integrative approaches to evaluate both legacy and emerging compounds.

articles.title: Changes in human biomarkers of exposure after complete switching from cigarettes to e-cigarettes or exclusive e-cigarette use: a systematic review and biomarker-specific meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Combustible cigarette smoking remains a major preventable cause of premature mortality worldwide, and the public-health relevance of electronic cigarettes depends substantially on whether switching from cigarettes lowers exposure to toxicants associated with smoking-related disease. We systematically reviewed the human biomonitoring evidence and quantified changes in biomarkers of exposure after complete switching from cigarettes to e-cigarettes or exclusive e-cigarette use after cigarette smoking. METHODS: PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection were searched from inception to 28 May 2026 for human studies reporting biomarkers of exposure or potential harm in relation to e-cigarette use, dual use or switching. Study characteristics, biomarker data and a pragmatic risk-of-bias and funding assessment were extracted in duplicate. Meta-analysis was restricted to biomarkers of exposure with at least two compatible estimates for complete switching or exclusive e-cigarette use after cigarette smoking; dual-use evidence was synthesised narratively. Effects were expressed as ratios of means comparing post-switch with baseline or reference cigarette-smoking levels and pooled using random-effects models with restricted maximum likelihood estimation. RESULTS: Sixty studies were included. Six publications, representing seven study-level sources, contributed 47 biomarker-specific effects across ten biomarkers. Complete switching or exclusive e-cigarette use after cigarette smoking was associated with lower levels of every pooled biomarker. Approximate reductions were 61% for NNAL, 92% for NNN, 72% for 3-HPMA, 84% for the acrylonitrile metabolite CEMA, 77% for HMPMA, 82% for MHBMA, 90% for S-PMA, 79% for exhaled carbon monoxide, 77% for carboxyhaemoglobin and 76% for 1-OHP. Between-study heterogeneity was substantial for most biomarkers (I² 57-99%), and 95% prediction intervals lay entirely below 1.0 only for NNN, CEMA and carboxyhaemoglobin; the pooled values are therefore central estimates rather than precise expectations for any individual future study. Narrative evidence was broadly consistent: exclusive e-cigarette use was generally associated with lower exposure than cigarette smoking, whereas reductions among dual users were smaller and depended on cigarette displacement. Biomarkers of potential harm were more heterogeneous and were not pooled. Many switching studies were short-term, product-specific and industry-funded. CONCLUSIONS: Complete switching from cigarettes to e-cigarettes or exclusive e-cigarette use after cigarette smoking is associated with substantially lower biomarkers of exposure to tobacco- and combustion-related toxicants. Exposure reductions appear greatest when cigarette smoking is fully displaced. These findings describe reduced exposure to measured toxicants; they do not, by themselves, establish reduced disease risk or long-term safety.

articles.title: Polyol Pathway Inhibition by Epalrestat Attenuates Pathological Bone Loss through Redox Homeostasis and Sorbitol-Linked Calcium Signaling.
articles.abstract: The contribution of polyol metabolism to pathological bone remodeling remains incompletely understood. Here, we examined its role in osteoclastogenesis and evaluated the skeletal effects of epalrestat, a clinically approved aldose reductase inhibitor. Exploratory single-cell analysis of two human femoral-head specimens suggested greater macrophage-associated polyol-pathway activity in the osteoporosis specimen. In primary bone marrow-derived macrophages, silencing of Akr1b3 and Sord produced opposing effects on osteoclast differentiation. Epalrestat suppressed RANKL-induced osteoclastogenesis and attenuated bone loss in diabetic, ovariectomy-induced, and inflammatory mouse models under early-intervention regimens. Mechanistic analyses showed improved NADPH/NADP⁺ and GSH/GSSG balance, reduced oxidative stress, and attenuated cytosolic and mitochondrial Ca²⁺ signals and Ca²⁺ oscillations. Genetic and osmotic-compensation experiments further supported a model in which intracellular sorbitol contributes to the osmotic regulation of Ca²⁺ oscillations. Additional findings included reduced inflammation in osteolysis and arthritis models, altered macrophage polarization, and partial preservation of bone marrow vascular features. Together, these findings connect glucose metabolism with redox and Ca²⁺ regulation during osteoclast differentiation and provide a rationale for further evaluation of epalrestat in skeletal disease.

articles.title: GABARAPL1 drives therapeutic differentiation of cancer cells by targeting epigenetic changes regulated by SFPQ.
articles.abstract: Differentiation-based cancer therapy is a potentially low-toxicity approach with demonstrated clinical benefits. However, the therapeutic efficacy of differentiation therapy remains limited in tumor types other than acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). Our previous studies reported that diptoindonesin G (Dip G), a natural compound, can induce differentiation in both acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells and basal-like breast cancer cells. In this study, we report a crucial role of GABAA receptor-associated protein-like 1 (GABARAPL1) in driving cancer cell differentiation. By utilizing myeloid cell differentiation models and primary leukemic cells, we demonstrate that upregulation of GABARAPL1 expression was crucial for Dip G-induced differentiation and that Dip G upregulated GABARAPL1 expression by targeting nucleolin (NCL). Also, GABARAPL1 promoted differentiation independent of its autophagic function. Both pharmacological and genetic upregulation of GABARAPL1 expression effectively overcame the differentiation blockade in various tumor models, including AML cells. Mechanistically, GABARAPL1 interacted with splicing factor proline and glutamine rich (SFPQ) and recruited MDM2 to promote the degradation of SFPQ by the proteasome. Upon SFPQ depletion, the transcription of linker histone H1.2 gene was repressed, which in turn rescued the transcription of the differentiation-related pathway. Our study not only highlights the contribution of GABARAPL1 to differentiation but also provides a potential therapeutic strategy aimed at expanding the scope of application of differentiation-based cancer therapy.

articles.title: Biodegradable radiopaque polymeric particles for computed tomography-guided intraperitoneal drug delivery.
articles.abstract: An iodinated hydrophobic oil containing the 2,3,5-triiodobenzoate moiety was encapsulated in biodegradable poly(lactic acid)-based polymer particles using a solvent emulsion-evaporation technique that provided control over particle size. The hydrophobic iodinated oil served a dual function as radiopaque contrast agent for particle quantification using dual-energy x-ray computed tomography (DECT) imaging and furthermore as solvent for the chemotherapeutic drug paclitaxel (PTX), establishing a novel theranostic system. Release kinetics of PTX was studied in fetal bovine serum over seven days demonstrating sustainable drug release over the entire period, with cumulative release mainly depending on particle diameter. Intraperitoneal administration of a therapeutic dosage of radiopaque spheres in mice provided sufficient iodine contrast to track biodistribution and clearance over 18 days. Importantly, imaging showed unexpected particle aggregation in vivo with about 50% clearance over 18 days, emphasizing the value of real-time distribution assessment as a complementary method to conventional ex-vivo histology. A proof of concept of longitudinal dual imaging using single-photon emission CT (SPECT)/DECT was demonstrated in a mouse model of colorectal cancer with intraperitoneal metastases following a single intraperitoneal dose of PTX or PTX-loaded particles. Treatment response was monitored using SPECT, while particle distribution was tracked by DECT. This theranostic approach integrates controlled intraperitoneal drug delivery with non-invasive quantitative DECT-based imaging and may improve treatment precision and therapeutic outcomes.

articles.title: Rationally designed negatively charged lipid nanoparticles reduce systemic reactogenicity of mRNA vaccines while preserving immunogenicity.
articles.abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines have emerged as versatile platforms for the prevention of infectious diseases and therapeutic cancer vaccination. However, strong reactogenicity remains a key challenge, with severe adverse events such as myocarditis. These concerns may limit the applications of mRNA vaccines. As lipid nanoparticles (LNP) are the primary driver of inflammation, optimizing LNP composition is a promising approach to reduce mRNA vaccine reactogenicity. However, the effects of tuning the physicochemical properties of LNP, particularly their surface charge, remain insufficiently characterized. In this study, we aimed to engineer negatively charged LNPs by incorporating anionic phospholipids and evaluate their biodistribution, immunogenicity, and adverse reactions in mice. Negatively charged LNPs significantly reduced systemic inflammatory responses and fever compared to a conventional LNP. Moreover, cardiac troponin I-a marker of myocarditis-was reduced in negatively charged LNPs. Despite reduced systemic reactogenicity, negatively charged LNPs maintained antigen-specific immunogenicity comparable to a conventional LNP. The negatively charged LNPs did not attenuate local inflammation at the injection site. This local inflammation depended on the fatty acyl chain of phospholipids in the LNP and was independent of the head group structure or negative charge. Surface charge modulation also reshaped biodistribution to distal organs, such as the spleen and liver. Correlation analysis linked reduced reactogenicity to decreased hepatic delivery of LNPs, and prior datasets supported this relationship. Taken together, our results establish phospholipid-driven surface-charge control as a promising approach to reduce systemic reactogenicity while maintaining the immunogenicity of mRNA vaccines.

articles.title: Reversal of tumor-immune metabolic competition via sequential energy blockade to reactivate exhausted T cells for enhanced cancer immunotherapy.
articles.abstract: The efficacy of cancer immunotherapy is usually constrained by tumor-immune metabolic competition. Metabolic blockade therapies face metabolic plasticity, whereas simultaneous drug delivery is limited by ATP-dependent drug and ion efflux. Herein, a tumor-microenvironment (TME)-activatable yolk-shell nanoreactor comprising a calcium peroxide (CP) core, a WZB117 (WZB)-loaded cavity, a hollow mesoporous Cu-3,3'-dithiobis(propionylhydrazine) shell (HMCT), and a hyaluronic acid (HA) coating (CP-WZB@HMCT@HA) was developed to execute a "starve-first, strike-later" sequential energy blockade strategy. A spatiotemporal cascade mediated by CP-WZB@HMCT@HA is activated under acidic and GSH-rich TME. Initially, disulfide-bridged shell degradation releases Cu species that deplete GSH, sensitizing tumor cells to oxidative stress. Crucially, glycolysis is inhibited by the early release of the GLUT1 inhibitor WZB, which leads to rapid ATP depletion that suppresses efflux pumps and increases intracellular retention of therapeutic agents. Subsequently, calcium overload and copper-mediated ROS generation disrupt mitochondrial homeostasis. This sequential energy blockade induces tumor energy depletion, elevates extracellular glucose levels, and reduces lactate accumulation. Consequently, immunosuppressive factors (PD-L1/TGF-β1) are downregulated, which reactivates the antitumor immune capacity of exhausted T cells. In vitro and in vivo assessments demonstrate antitumor activity and acceptable biocompatibility. This strategy provides a potential approach for remodeling tumor-immune metabolic competition and improving cancer immunotherapy.

articles.title: Targeting V-ATPase assembly via sEVs-delivered doxorubicin triggers methuosis and circumvents temozolomide resistance in glioblastoma.
articles.abstract: AIM: Temozolomide (TMZ) resistance remains a major challenge in glioblastoma (GBM). Whether lysosomal alterations represent a targetable vulnerability in TMZ-resistant GBM (TR-GBM) is unclear. This study investigates whether small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) can reprogram doxorubicin (DOX) subcellular trafficking to exploit lysosomal vulnerabilities and circumvent resistance. METHODS: Paired primary/recurrent GBM tissues, TR-GBM cell lines (TR-U87, TR-U251), patient-derived xenografts (PDX), and orthotopic models were used. DOX-loaded sEVs (sEVs-DOX) were characterized. Subcellular DOX distribution was assessed by confocal microscopy, organelle staining, and Percoll gradient fractionation. V-ATPase assembly and function were evaluated by co-immunoprecipitation, immunofluorescence, lysosomal pH measurement, and proton-pumping activity. ATP6V1D overexpression and knockdown were used for validation. RESULTS: TR-GBM showed lysosomal expansion and instability. sEVs-DOX redirected DOX to lysosomes, inducing methuosis and circumventing TMZ resistance. Mechanistically, lysosomal DOX directly bound ATP6V1D, disrupting V-ATPase assembly, causing lysosomal deacidification and dysfunction. ATP6V1D overexpression rescued these defects, whereas knockdown phenocopied sEVs-DOX effects. sEVs-DOX demonstrated potent efficacy in subcutaneous, orthotopic, and PDX models with minimal toxicity. CONCLUSION: Lysosomal dysfunction is a targetable vulnerability in TR-GBM. sEVs-DOX circumvents resistance by inducing V-ATPase-dependent methuosis, offering a promising therapeutic strategy.

articles.title: Ginkgolide B drives cardiomyocyte proliferation and myocardial regeneration through TLR4/NF-κB/HIF-1α-regulated glycolytic reprogramming.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Myocardial infarction (MI) continues to contribute substantially to global mortality and is characterized by irreversible cardiomyocyte loss and limited regenerative capacity in the adult heart. Ginkgolide B (GB), a bioactive compound used in traditional Chinese medicine, has well-documented cardioprotective effects; however, whether it promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation and myocardial regeneration, and through which mechanisms, remains unclear. PURPOSE: This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential and underlying molecular mechanisms of GB in promoting cardiomyocyte proliferation and cardiac regeneration. METHODS: The therapeutic effects of GB were assessed in cardiomyocyte (CM) cell lines and mouse models of apical resection (AR) and MI. To define the underlying mechanism, we combined network pharmacology, molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, RNA sequencing, and targeted metabolite profiling. The interaction between GB and TLR4 was evaluated using a cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA). The dependency on the TLR4/NF-κB/HIF-1α pathway and glycolysis were pharmacologically validated using 2-deoxy-d-glucose (2-DG, glycolysis inhibitor) and Bay 11-7082 (NF-κB inhibitor). RESULTS: GB enhanced CM proliferation and angiogenesis in vitro, and improved cardiac function, reduced infarct size, and promoted CM proliferation in neonatal and adult mouse models. Mechanistically, GB interacted directly with TLR4, activated the NF-κB/HIF-1α signaling axis, and promoted a shift toward glycolytic metabolism. Inhibition of NF-κB or glycolysis abolished GB-induced CM proliferation, glycolytic activity, and myocardial regeneration. CONCLUSIONS: GB promotes cardiomyocyte proliferation and cardiac regeneration through TLR4/NF-κB/HIF-1α-dependent regulation of glycolytic metabolism. These findings support the potential of GB as a plant-derived therapeutic candidate for ischemic heart disease.

articles.title: Dihydrotanshinone I suppresses ovarian cancer by targeting splicing factor SRSF1 to regulate the long non-coding RNA SLC8A1-AS1/FOXO1 axis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ovarian cancer (OC) is a lethal malignancy with limited therapies. The natural compound dihydrotanshinone I (DHT) exhibits broad antitumor activity, yet its precise molecular targets and mechanistic interplay with oncogenic lncRNAs in OC remain largely unexplored. PURPOSE: This study aimed to investigate the molecular targets and underlying mechanisms of DHT‑regulated lncRNAs in OC. STUDY DESIGN: DHT efficacy was evaluated in vitro and in vivo. Mechanisms were investigated via lncRNA profiling, transcriptomic analysis, functional assays, and protein‑binding experiments. METHODS: The antitumor efficacy of DHT was assessed in OC cells and xenograft models. LncRNA candidates were screened using microarray and validated by clinical cohort analysis. The regulatory role of SLC8A1-AS1 was further verified through functional assays. RNA pull-down/MS and RIP were performed to identify proteins binding to SLC8A1-AS1. Rescue experiments were conducted to evaluate whether SRSF1 influences SLC8A1-AS1 stability. The DHT-SRSF1 interaction and binding sites were examined through SPR, CETSA, DARTS, MS, and molecular docking. Transcriptomics and western blot were conducted to analyze downstream signaling cascades. RESULTS: DHT significantly suppressed OC growth. SLC8A1-AS1 was highly expressed and associated with poor prognosis in OC. Mechanistically, SRSF1 bound to SLC8A1-AS1 and enhanced its stability, activating the PI3K/AKT/FOXO1 pathway. DHT directly bound to SRSF1 and induced its degradation, downregulating SLC8A1-AS1 expression and inactivating the pathway, ultimately suppressing proliferation in OC. CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies SLC8A1-AS1 as a novel prognostic biomarker in OC and provides the first evidence that DHT exerts its antitumor effects by targeting the SRSF1/SLC8A1-AS1/FOXO1 axis. These findings unveil the role of SLC8A1-AS1 in OC progression and elucidate the mechanistic basis for the therapeutic potential of DHT.

articles.title: A small molecule utilizes both antivirulence and host-directed mechanisms to combat bacterial infection.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Antimicrobial resistance is progressively undermining the efficacy of conventional antibiotics, and intracellular infections caused by Salmonella typhimurium (ST) remain difficult to eradicate, underscoring the need for alternative therapeutic strategies. PURPOSE: To identify natural small molecules possessing both antivirulence and host-directed activities against ST infection, and further characterize their mechanisms of action. METHODS: A dual-screening strategy was employed to identify compounds that inhibit both ST invasion and intracellular replication. RNA sequencing, quantitative polymerase chain reaction, western blot analysis, β-galactosidase reporter assay, scanning electron microscopy, and flow cytometry were performed to investigate the mode of action of the active compound. A murine enterocolitis model was established to evaluate its therapeutic efficacy. RESULTS: Ferulic acid (FA) emerged as a dual-acting inhibitor. FA suppressed SPI-4 promoter PsiiA activity, reduced SPI-4 transcription and SiiE secretion, and impaired SiiE-dependent adhesion, thereby limiting bacterial invasion. In parallel, FA suppressed macrophage STAT3 phosphorylation and enhanced NRF2 signaling, leading to reduced intracellular ferrous iron and ferroptosis, which in turn restricted intracellular bacterial replication. Furthermore, FA treatment alleviated ST-induced enterocolitis in mice. CONCLUSIONS: FA protects against ST infection by attenuating bacterial virulence and modulating host iron homeostasis. These findings support its potential as a combined antivirulence and host-directed therapeutic candidate.

articles.title: Vusolimogene Oderparepvec: First Approval.
articles.abstract: Vusolimogene oderparepvec (TUDRIQEV™; vusolimogene oderparepvec-wtpg) is a genetically modified oncolytic viral therapy that targets cancer cells. It is being developed by Replimune for the treatment of skin malignancies and received its first approval for combination treatment with nivolumab on 6 August 2026 in the USA. The combination of vusolimogene oderparepvec and nivolumab resulted in objective responses in patients with unresectable advanced melanoma after progression with an anti-PD-1 regimen during the IGNYTE phase I/II trial. This article summarises the milestones in the development of vusolimogene oderparepvec leading to this first approval in combination with nivolumab for the treatment of adult patients with unresectable advanced cutaneous melanoma who experienced disease progression with a PD-1-blocking antibody-based regimen.

articles.title: Centanafadine: First Approval.
articles.abstract: Centanafadine (SIMTRIYO®) is a first-in-class, sustained-release norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin reuptake inhibitor and central nervous system stimulant developed by Otsuka Pharmaceutical for the treatment of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Centanafadine recently received approval in the USA for the treatment of ADHD in adult patients and paediatric patients aged ≥ 6 years weighing ≥ 20 kg. This article summarizes the milestones in the development of centanafadine leading to this first approval for ADHD in adult and paediatric patients.

articles.title: Plasma EC90 multiples are drug, target site and species specific-A physiologically based pharmacokinetic modelling example of nirmatrelvir central nervous system distribution.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Achieving minimum unbound drug concentration in plasma above in vitro EC90 is a common antiviral pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) target. However, it often overlooks restricted distribution into target sites like the central nervous system (CNS), where a trough concentration above 1 × EC90 is needed. Currently, the required EC90 multiplier (n) is defined empirically without mechanistic evidence. This study utilizes physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modelling of nirmatrelvir in rats to bridge the gap between plasma and target-site exposure, providing a mechanistic basis for the minimal EC90 multiplier in antiviral dose selection. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: A nirmatrelvir population PK (popPK) model developed from rat plasma data was integrated into the LeiCNS PBPK platform. Evaluated against rat cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) concentration, the PBPK model was used to simulate drug distribution across various CNS compartments, to assess the plasma-to-periphery relationship of antivirals with varying blood-brain barrier (BBB) permeability. KEY RESULTS: The simulation results highlight how both unbound fraction in plasma (fu) and unbound tissue-to-plasma partition coefficient (Kp,uu) are the primary determinants of the minimal EC90 multiplier. We demonstrated that aiming to reach plasma Cmin above an arbitrary multiple of the EC90 without accounting for drug and species-dependent parameters, and related body distribution, can lead to insufficient drug exposure at peripheral target sites. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: Target-site concentration, rather than total plasma concentration, is the mechanistically correct effect site for linking to in vitro EC90. By incorporating both fu and Kp,uu, a more mechanistically informed EC90 multiplier can be predicted a priori.

articles.title: Impact of clinical pharmacist interventions in psychiatric hospitals on clinical and medication-related outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Clinical pharmacist interventions have been shown to improve outcomes and reduce drug-related problems (DRPs) in patients with mental disorders. However, no previous meta-analysis has comprehensively evaluated their effectiveness in reducing DRPs and optimizing pharmacotherapy in psychiatric inpatient settings. AIM: To evaluate the effectiveness of clinical pharmacist interventions in psychiatric inpatient settings on DRPs and clinical outcomes among patients with mental disorders. METHODS: This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to the PRISMA 2020 statement and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261309290). PubMed, Scopus, CENTRAL, and CINAHL were searched from inception to March 2026. Eligible studies included adult psychiatric inpatients receiving clinical pharmacist interventions, including different pharmaceutical services, such as medication review, medication reconciliation, and ward round participation. A meta-analysis was performed in R using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was calculated using I2. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed for DRPs, potentially inappropriate medications (PIMs), and the number of prescribed medications. Risk of bias was assessed using RoB two and ROBINS-I. RESULTS: Eighteen studies met the inclusion criteria, including one randomized controlled trial and 17 non-randomized interventional studies. Clinical pharmacist interventions significantly reduced the number of prescribed medications (mean difference -1.0 medications per patient, (95% CI -1.5 to -0.5) and were associated with a pooled reduction in DRPs of 70.7% (95% CI 46.5-87.0), as well as reductions in PIMs. Evidence for patient-centred clinical outcomes, including symptom improvement, quality of life, and healthcare utilization, remained limited. Substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies, reflecting differences in intervention types, patient populations, and outcome measures. Most non-randomized studies were judged to have a serious risk of bias because of confounding and uncontrolled study designs. CONCLUSION: Clinical pharmacist interventions in psychiatric inpatient settings improve medication-related outcomes by reducing DRPs, PIMs, and the number of prescribed medications. These findings support the integration of clinical pharmacists into multidisciplinary psychiatric teams. Further adequately powered multicentre randomized controlled trials are needed to determine whether these improvements translate into better long-term patient-centred clinical outcomes.

articles.title: Selected traditional Chinese medicines for treating amyotrophic lateral sclerosis: a Bayesian network meta-analysis based on randomised controlled trials.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To assess the effectiveness of specific Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) therapies for Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) using Bayesian network meta-analysis. METHODS: PubMed, the Cochrane Library, EMBASE, Web of Science, and four Chinese databases up to 15th December 2024 was searched, including RCTs on adult Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis patients treated with TCM therapies (Chinese herbal medicine, preparations, non-pharmacological treatments) alone or combined with conventional treatments. Controls included no intervention, placebo, conventional treatments, or combinations. Primary outcomes were functional status (ALSFRS, ALSFRS-R, AALSS, m-Norris scales). Bayesian network meta-analysis compared treatment effects and calculated SUCRA values. RESULTS: Thirty-five RCTs involving 27 TCM therapies were included. No significant differences in functional status or quality of life were found among TCM therapies, ICT, Riluzole alone, and Riluzole plus placebo. For functional status, Shenmai injection + ICT (SUCRA 0.735 for ALSFRS, 0.870 for ALSFRS-R), Jiweiling injection + placebo (SUCRA 0.868 for ALSFRS), Jiawei Sijunzi decoction alone (SUCRA 0.739 for ALSFRS-R), Acupuncture + rehabilitation exercises + Riluzole (SUCRA 0.928 for AALSS, 0.863 for m-Norris) and Shenzhe Jiangqi powder + placebo (SUCRA 0.860 for m-Norris) had the highest probabilities of being superior treatment. For quality of life, Thunder fire moxibustion + Riluzole and Jiweiling injection + placebo for ALSAQ-40 were favorable. CONCLUSION: Despite no significant differences in functional status among TCM therapies, ICT, Riluzole alone, and Riluzole plus placebo, Jiweiling injection, Shenmai injection, Jiawei Sijunzi decoction, and Shenzhe Jiangqi powder may be regarded as candidate preparations for ALS patients. Future research should focus on real-world data to explore long-term effects and practical benefits. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://inplasy.com/inplasy-2024-8-0050/, identifier INPLASY202480050.

articles.title: Mapping the intellectual landscape of lactylation research: a bibliometric analysis of global trends and emerging frontiers.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lactylation is an emerging post-translational modification (PTM) that links lactate metabolism with epigenetic and protein-level regulation. The rapid expansion of this field has created a need for a systematic overview of its knowledge structure and research frontiers. METHODS: We retrieved 1,231 English articles and reviews from the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus up to 7 November 2025. Excel, CiteSpace, VOSviewer, and Bibliometrix were used to analyze publication trends, collaboration networks, influential contributors, co-cited references, and keyword evolution. RESULTS: Annual publications and citations increased sharply after 2019. China and the United States were the two major contributors in publication output and collaboration networks. Advanced Science and Frontiers in Immunology were prominent publication venues, and authors including Xu K, Zhao YM, Huang H, and Zhang D showed high bibliometric visibility. Co-citation and keyword analyses identified two major research axes: lactylation in cancer biology, tumor immune regulation, and therapy resistance; and lactylation in metabolic reprogramming and disease-associated stress responses. CONCLUSION: Lactylation research is moving from site discovery toward mechanistic studies of pathophysiological regulation. The present bibliometric map provides a quantitative framework for understanding the field, while emphasizing that current translational claims remain largely preclinical and require further mechanistic and biomarker validation.

articles.title: Effects and potential mechanisms of si-ni-san on animal models of depression: a preclinical systematic review and meta-analysis.
articles.abstract: CONTEXT: In Traditional Chinese Medicine depressive disorders are commonly associated with liver qi stagnation syndrome. Si-ni-san (SNS), a classic formula for soothing the liver and relieving qi stagnation, is widely used for its potential antidepressant-like effects. OBJECTIVE: This preclinical systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the pharmacological effects of SNS on depression-related behavioral outcomes in animal models and to summarize its mechanisms of action. METHODS: We conducted a systematic search of seven databases (including PubMed) for records published up to December 2025. Risk of bias was assessed using SYRCLE's tool. Meta-analyses were performed using STATA 15.0 and RevMan 5.4. Subgroup and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were conducted to test the robustness of the findings. Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger's test. Trim-and-fill analysis was performed to adjust for potential publication bias. The certainty of evidence was evaluated using a modified GRADE approach for preclinical studies. RESULTS: A total of 28 studies were included, involving 384 animals and three behavioral tests: sucrose preference test (SPT), forced swim test (FST), and tail suspension test (TST). SNS treatment was associated with increased sucrose preference in the SPT (SMD = 3.18, 95% CI = [2.44, 3.93]), and reduced immobility time in both the FST (SMD = -2.17, 95% CI = [-2.86, -1.49]) and TST (SMD = -2.55, 95% CI = [-3.31, -1.78]). Mechanistically, SNS treatment was associated with increased monoamine neurotransmitters (MNTs), reduced hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis hormones, and decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines. CONCLUSION: These findings suggest that SNS is associated with antidepressant-like pharmacological effects in rodent models, with changes in MNTs, HPA axis hormones, and inflammatory markers. However, due to substantial heterogeneity, risk of bias, and inadequate phytochemical characterization, these results should be considered hypothesis-generating and interpreted with caution.

articles.title: Carrier-free self-assembled nanodrugs in cancer therapy: a systematic scoping review and evidence map of molecular architecture, drug resistance, and translation-relevant reporting.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Carrier-free self-assembled nanodrugs use therapeutic or bioactive molecules as principal structural components. Their architectures have diversified rapidly, but how molecular design relates to resistance evidence and further development remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To map molecular architecture, drug-resistance evidence, and translation-relevant reporting in carrier-free anticancer nanodrugs. METHODS: We conducted a PRISMA-ScR systematic scoping review and evidence map integrated with bibliometric analysis and structured appraisal of key resistance studies. PubMed, Europe PMC, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection (WoSCC) were searched in August 2026. WoSCC records (n = 863) characterized publication and intellectual structure, Scopus records (n = 840) assessed coverage, and 526 eligible articles formed the evidence map. Architecture was classified in 481 original studies, resistance evidence in 160 records, and 19 translation-relevant domains in 147 full-text studies. All 43 Tier 1/2 studies underwent full-report appraisal. RESULTS: Covalent prodrug/conjugate assemblies (n = 187) and noncovalent multi-active co-assemblies (n = 182) predominated. Of 160 resistance-related records, 28 used established resistant models (Tier 1), whereas 15 provided mechanism-aligned sensitization evidence without resistant-model confirmation (Tier 2). Architecture was not clearly associated with Tier one versus Tier 2 classification in exploratory analysis (Cramér's V = 0.394, Holm-adjusted P = 0.666). In the 147-study full-text subset, batch consistency and experimental scalability were each reported in three studies and long-term toxicity in four. Seven studies met the composite human-related evidence domain, but only one involved direct clinical administration (1/147, 0.7%). After excluding incomplete 2026 data, the latest-versus-earliest difference in reporting completeness was 1.40 domains (95% CI, -0.49-3.25), providing no clear evidence of sustained temporal improvement. CONCLUSION: Carrier-free anticancer nanodrugs have diversified rapidly, but evidence supporting resistance and further development has not matured in parallel. By separating resistance mechanism from evidentiary strength and distinguishing resistant-model validation from mechanism-aligned sensitization, this review establishes clearer boundaries for resistance claims and identifies manufacturing reproducibility, long-term safety, and direct clinical evaluation as major evidence gaps. The resulting framework provides a practical basis for aligning molecular design with claim-specific pharmacology and development-oriented evidence generation.

articles.title: Comparative effectiveness and safety of almonertinib in EGFR-mutated non-small cell lung cancer: an integrated evidence synthesis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Comparative evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of almonertinib in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) remains fragmented across randomized and real-world studies. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to comprehensively evaluate the comparative clinical performance of almonertinib. METHODS: Eight electronic databases were systematically searched from inception to March 2025. Comparative studies evaluating almonertinib versus active control regimens in patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC were included. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed to synthesize objective response rate (ORR), disease control rate (DCR), progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and treatment-related adverse events. Methodological quality was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool and analogous domains for observational studies, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework. RESULTS: Fifteen comparative studies involving 1,902 patients met the eligibility criteria. Compared with control regimens, almonertinib was associated with higher pooled ORR (RR = 1.33, 95% CI 1.08-1.65) and DCR (RR = 1.14, 95% CI 1.03-1.26). However, after trim-and-fill adjustment for potential publication bias, the 95% CIs for both ORR and DCR included the null value, suggesting that the observed response benefits may be influenced by small-study effects. No statistically significant differences were observed for pooled PFS or OS. Almonertinib demonstrated a generally favorable safety profile, with a lower incidence of diarrhea, while rates of grade ≥3 adverse events and other major toxicities were broadly comparable between groups. Integrated analyses further suggested consistent concordance between ORR and DCR across most studies, supporting improved short-term disease control despite moderate-to-substantial between-study heterogeneity. CONCLUSION: Current comparative evidence suggests that almonertinib may improve tumor response and disease control while maintaining a favorable tolerability profile in patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC. Although favorable objective response outcomes were observed, these benefits may be influenced by small-study effects, and definitive survival advantages remain uncertain. These findings support almonertinib as a clinically meaningful therapeutic option, while underscoring the need for cautious interpretation and for larger, high-quality comparative trials with longer follow-up to further define its long-term clinical value. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/ZDF2N; Identifier: OSF.IO/ZDF2N.

articles.title: Investigating the TASK1 potassium channel in equine atrial myocardium as a potential treatment target for atrial fibrillation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common clinically relevant arrhythmia in horses, with limited pharmacological treatment options in both veterinary and human medicine. TASK1 potassium channels represent a promising atrial-selective antiarrhythmic target, but their relevance in horses has not been established. To characterize equine TASK1 (eqTASK1) channels regarding structural conservation, electrophysiological function, pharmacological sensitivity, cardiac expression pattern and in vivo electrophysiological effects of TASK1 inhibition. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Sixteen horses killed for non-cardiovascular reasons, of which 10 horses used for tissue harvesting and six horses for in vivo testing. Functional and pharmacological properties of eq TASK1 and human (hTASK1) channels were assessed in Xenopus laevis oocytes using two-electrode voltage clamp recordings. Cardiac expression of eqTASK1 was analysed by qRT-PCR and immunoblotting, while in vivo electrophysiological studies were performed in anaesthetized horses before and after intravenous ketodoxapram administration. KEY RESULTS: EqTASK1 and h TASK1 channels demonstrated high structural conservation, comparable potassium-selective background currents and preserved pharmacological sensitivity with species-dependent differences in potency. EqTASK1 expression was strongly enriched in atrial and nodal tissue, whereas ventricular expression was minimal. In vivo administration of ketodoxapram significantly prolonged atrial effective refractory periods from 275 ± 54 to 418 ± 94 ms without significant changes in heart rate or atrioventricular conduction parameters. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: EqTASK1 channels are highly conserved with human orthologs and display pronounced atrial-predominant cardiac expression. In vivo TASK1 inhibition prolongs atrial refractoriness in horses, supporting TASK1 as a translational atrial-selective antiarrhythmic target in both human and veterinary medicine.

articles.title: Cheminformatics-based read-across prioritization of food additives with obesogenic potential and PPARγ agonist activity.
articles.abstract: Food additives are widely used in processed foods, yet many remain insufficiently evaluated for potential metabolic-disrupting effects. In this study, we developed a cheminformatics-based read-across approach integrating curated food additive inventories with Tox21 high-throughput screening (HTS) data to prioritize food additives with potential obesogenic activity. We integrated 7917 compounds from the Tox21 dataset with 3185 compounds from curated food additive inventories, followed by rigorous data curation to yield a dataset comprising 10,077 compounds. Dimensionality reduction and clustering analyses identified 428 structurally defined clusters. Enrichment analysis of Tox21 assay endpoints identified five clusters significantly associated with peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor γ (PPARγ) agonist activity. From these PPARγ activity-enriched clusters, eight food additives not previously evaluated in Tox21 were prioritized for experimental validation and assessed in an adipogenic differentiation model of human bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (hBM-MSCs). Among them, benzyl disulfide (BD), hesperetin (HSP), and syringaldehyde (SD) significantly enhanced adiponectin biosynthesis and lipid accumulation. Pharmacological profiling further demonstrated that BD and HSP directly bound to PPARγ and induced coactivator recruitment. Collectively, these findings support the use of integrated cheminformatics read-across analysis and targeted in vitro testing for hazard identification and prioritization of food additives with potential obesogenic activity. The results provide a basis for further mechanistic and exposure-informed assessment of the prioritized candidates.

articles.title: Environmentally relevant bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate exposure increases stress vulnerability, evoking depressive-like behaviors in male mice.
articles.abstract: Chronic stress is a major risk factor for major depressive disorder, and accumulating evidence implicates environmental pollutants in depression-related pathophysiology. We previously showed that prolonged exposure to bis(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate (DEHP) induces depressive-like behaviors in male mice by dampening glutamatergic transmission in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), resembling the effects shown in the chronic immobilization stress (CIS)-induced mouse model of depression. Here, we investigated whether chronic environmentally relevant (ER) DEHP exposure increases vulnerability to stress. Mice received DEHP (120-125 µg/kg body weight) for 42 days and were then subjected to a subthreshold immobilization stress (sIS) regimen that does not elicit overt depressive-like behaviors when administered alone. Notably, DEHP exposure rendered this otherwise subthreshold stress sufficient to unmask a robust depressive-like phenotype. Mice exposed to DEHP + sIS displayed anxiety-like, despair/helplessness-like, and anhedonia-like behaviors, along with elevated corticosterone and reactive oxygen/nitrogen species, recapitulating key features observed in mice with CIS-induced depression. Mechanistically, mice exposed to DEHP + sIS and to CIS both exhibited reduced glutamatergic signaling and decreased glutamine synthetase activity in the mPFC. Together, these findings indicate that sustained ER pollutant exposure can sensitize stress responses and lower the threshold for stress-evoked depressive-like behaviors, and that the underappreciated interaction between environmental pollutants and psychosocial stressors warrants closer attention in assessments of mental health risk.

articles.title: Development and translational application of a rat-to-human PBPK model for isopropoxate to support forensic exposure reconstruction and risk assessment.
articles.abstract: Isopropoxate is a new synthetic etomidate analog and emerging new psychoactive substance, posing severe public health risks due to its high abuse liability and overdose potential. Ethical constraints preclude clinical pharmacokinetic investigations, necessitating alternative mechanistic approaches. In this study, we developed the first physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) model for isopropoxate by integrating in vitro data of human liver microsomes and in vivo data of rats. The rat PBPK model accurately described dose-dependent plasma concentration-time profiles, with predicted-to-observed ratios remaining within the accepted two-fold range, as reflected by fold errors (FE) of 0.944-1.12 for Cmax and 0.744-1.68 for AUC0-∞ across all dose levels. In addition, dedicated PBPK submodels were established and validated for the primary metabolite of etomidate acid with FE ranging from 0.800 to 1.01 for Cmax. Human pharmacokinetics were extrapolated using in vitro-in vivo extrapolation (IVIVE) and allometric scaling, predicting a high oral bioavailability of 94.9% and a systemic clearance of 0.31 mL/min/kg. The model facilitates pharmacokinetic interpretation, postmortem back-calculation of exposure timing, and assessment of metabolite production, thereby supporting forensic and overdose risk evaluation. Beyond predicting pharmacokinetics, the developed PBPK framework provides a practical tool for forensic toxicology by supporting interpretation of parent-metabolite relationships in biological specimens, reconstruction of exposure timelines under different scenarios, and mechanistic comparison of exposure profiles following different routes of administration.

articles.title: Evaluation of anogenital distance (AGD) and areola/nipple retention (NR) assessments in extended one generation reproductive toxicity studies - Implications for regulatory toxicology.
articles.abstract: The Extended One-Generation Reproductive Toxicity Study (EOGRTS) represents the current state-of-the-art in in vivo reproductive toxicity testing. Although its main purpose is to provide information on sexual function and fertility, it can also provide important information for assessing the endocrine disrupting effects of chemical substances. In a collaborative effort between the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) and nine EU Member States, a comprehensive review of the EOGRTS was conducted to evaluate its role in supporting regulatory hazard assessment in the EU. In a satellite project, measurements of anogenital distance (AGD) and areola/nipple retention (NR), two critical and sensitive endpoints in assessing endocrine disruption, were analysed. From 72 full study reports (FSR), all F1 generation offspring were investigated for AGD and NR. An additional 25 datasets for AGD and 21 datasets for NR were available from the F2 generation offspring, resulting in a total of 97 datasets analysed for AGD and 93 datasets for NR. In the evaluation of the AGD data, the following factors were assessed; coefficient of variation (CoV), measuring precision and overlap between male and female AGDs in the control group. Good or acceptable data quality (i.e. low CoV, sufficient measuring precision and a clear separation between male and female AGDs) was observed in 63% of the datasets. Limited data quality was seen in 12%, while 25% demonstrated insufficient quality. The 20 test facilities performing the studies demonstrated variable proficiency, with approximately one-third of the facilities excelling, one-third showing mixed results, and one-third underperforming. In the evaluation of the areola retention datasets, it was considered a potential limitation if no areolae were seen in any of the investigated males within a study. Likewise, a potential limitation was identified if an unexpectedly high number of areolae was seen in the control males. Surprisingly, these issues were very common and were identified in 83% of the datasets, which emphasises the importance of improving guidance on the assessment of this endpoint. Based on this review, updated guidance for assessing both endpoints is presently being prepared at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). Addressing the identified challenges will be crucial for enhancing the utility of the EOGRTS and consequently contributing to more informed decision-making on the potential hazards and risks associated with exposure to endocrine disrupting chemicals.

articles.title: Murine hippocampal CA3 vulnerability to intravenously administered polystyrene nanoplastics: preferential accumulation and ROS-related neuronal cell death.
articles.abstract: Polystyrene nanoplastics (PS-NPs) are emerging neurotoxicants with the potential to access the brain following systemic exposure; however, their region-specific effects and underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood. In this study, adult male mice (C57BL/6J) were intravenously injected with unlabeled or fluorescently labeled PS-NPs (50-60 nm) at a dose of 400 mg/kg, and brain tissues were collected and analyzed 3 days post-injection to evaluate PS-NPs distribution, oxidative stress, and regulated cell death pathways. Confocal imaging revealed preferential accumulation of fluorescent PS-NPs in the hippocampal CA3 region, where neuronal localization was most prominent among the regions examined. This accumulation was associated with a significant reduction in NeuN-positive neurons in CA3 (p < 0.01), accompanied by elevated mitochondrial ROS levels as detected by MitoSOX staining (p < 0.001). Immunofluorescence analyses demonstrated increased expression of cleaved caspase-3 and p-MLKL, indicating activation of apoptosis and necroptosis, whereas NLRP3 expression remained unchanged. Behavioral assessments using the Y-maze and passive avoidance tests revealed impairments in hippocampus-dependent cognitive performance in PS-NP-treated mice. Collectively, these findings suggest that acute intravenous exposure to PS-NPs induces early, region-selective neuronal vulnerability in the hippocampal CA3 area, which is associated with oxidative stress-mediated neuronal cell death and cognitive dysfunction under the present experimental conditions.

articles.title: Molecular basis of azole fungicide interactions with human estrogen receptor alpha (ERα): an integrated in silico and in vitro toxicological assessment.
articles.abstract: The extensive agricultural use of azole fungicides, while essential for crop protection, has raised growing concern regarding their potential to disrupt endocrine signaling in humans. This study examined the molecular basis of interactions between selected azole compounds and human estrogen receptor alpha (ERα) to determine their capacity to interfere with receptor function. An integrated in silico and in vitro workflow was employed. Molecular docking was first performed for the azoles alongside the endogenous agonist estradiol (E2) and the antagonist 4-hydroxytamoxifen (OHT) as reference ligands, followed by binding free energy estimation using MM/GBSA analysis. The five top-ranked azoles were subsequently characterized through ADMET profiling and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to assess their physicochemical and electronic properties. Molecular dynamics simulations and post-simulation MM/GBSA analysis were then conducted to evaluate the stability and dynamic behavior of the azole-ERα complexes. Experimental validation was performed using a bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET)-based assay. Computational analyses identified five azoles with notable binding affinity toward ERα, and molecular dynamics simulations confirmed the structural stability of the corresponding complexes, supported by favorable MM/GBSA binding energies. Experimentally, three azoles (flusilazole, myclobutanil, and tebuconazole) intrinsically induced cytosolic ERα dimerization, consistent with agonist-like activity, whereas the remaining two azoles (fenbuconazole and paclobutrazol) significantly suppressed E2-induced ERα dimerization, consistent with antagonist-like activity comparable to that produced by OHT. Together, these findings provide mechanistic insight into ERα modulation by azole fungicides and highlight their relevance for human endocrine toxicity and health risk assessment.

articles.title: Risk assessment of oral exposure to cyclic siloxanes - octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane (D4) as an example.
articles.abstract: Published data on in vivo toxicity of octamethylcyclotetrasiloxane (D4) on rat kidneys was re-evaluated. It turned out that a molecular and biochemical mode of action (MOA) of D4 induced effects on kidneys and its human relevance is missing, which remains a gap in current knowledge. Increased kidney weights (also in recovery groups) were considered as D4 specific adverse effects. In vitro, cytotoxicity was observed for D4 in human (HEK293, CaKi-1) and canine (MDCK) kidney cell lines, while no toxicity was observed in human hepatic cell line HepG2. Proteomic profiling at low toxic doses, using KEGG pathway analysis revealed that proteins in ribosomes, t-RNA biosynthesis and carbon metabolism were down-regulated in HEK293 cells. This indicates, that main cellular processes were disturbed. In HepG2 cells, DNA replication was affected, but no decrease in cell viability occurred. A BMDL5 value of 84 ppm for the kidney weight increases after chronic inhalation of D4 in rats was derived. The BMDL5 was converted to an oral TDI of 0.21 mg/kg bw per day, using standard factors. This corresponds to a specific migration reference value of 13 mg/kg food, which is applicable for food contact materials. Due to missing data on higher cyclic siloxane oligomers, but an expected similar toxicological profile, this reference value was applied to the weighed sum of oligomers from D4 to D13. The daily oral uptake of cyclic siloxanes was calculated, based on published migration and food consumption data. In summary, post-curing of food contact materials made of silicone reduced the exposure of D4 and higher oligomers below the specific migration reference value of 13 mg/kg food.

articles.title: Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6)-mediated α-tubulin (K40) deacetylation and microtubule destabilization disrupt autophagosome-lysosome fusion in PBDE-47-induced neurotoxicity.
articles.abstract: 2,2',4,4'-tetrabromodiphenyl ether (PBDE-47) is a pervasive environmental brominated flame retardant that accumulates in nervous tissues and induces persistent neurotoxicity. Emerging evidence indicates that PBDE-47 perturbs neuronal autophagy, yet the definitive upstream molecular mechanism remains uncharacterized, hindering the development of effective protective strategies. This study was performed to clarify the toxic regulatory cascade and explore feasible pharmacological interventions using in vivo neonatal rat hippocampal tissue and in vitro PC12 neuronal cell models. Animals were neonatally exposed to PBDE-47 (0.1, 1.0, 10.0 mg/kg·bw), and PC12 cells were treated with PBDE-47 (1, 10, 20 µM) for mechanistic exploration. Results showed that PBDE-47 dose-dependently upregulated histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), decreased α-tubulin (K40) acetylation, and destabilized neuronal microtubules. Such microtubule structural damage impaired autophagosome retrograde trafficking, blocked autophagosome-lysosome fusion, and eventually caused neuronal loss, synaptic protein reduction, and cognitive impairment. For mechanism validation and rescue experiments, 1 mg/kg·bw paclitaxel (PTX) and 1 mg/kg·bw tubastatin A (TBA) were administered to neonatal rats, whereas 12.5 nmol/L PTX and 10 µmol/L TBA were used for PC12 cell treatment to stabilize microtubules and selectively inhibit HDAC6, respectively. Both pharmacological interventions effectively restored tubulin acetylation, rescued defective autophagic flux, and mitigated PBDE-47-induced neuronal injury, with TBA showing better applicability due to its high blood-brain barrier permeability and biosafety. Behavioral tests in vivo verified that PTX and TBA treatment significantly ameliorated PBDE-47-elicited learning and memory deficits. Collectively, these findings define the HDAC6/microtubule acetylation axis as a core upstream pathway responsible for PBDE-47-triggered autophagic transport failure and neurotoxicity, providing robust experimental evidence and a promising therapeutic target for the prevention of PBDEs-mediated neurological disorders.

articles.title: Target fishing in the "kinome": integrated in silico/in vitro discovery of novel kinase inhibitory activities of alternariol.
articles.abstract: Alternariol (AOH), an emerging mycotoxin produced by Alternaria species, is a frequent contaminant of plant-derived foods and a major contributor to chronic dietary exposure to Alternaria toxins. Despite evidence of its cytotoxic, genotoxic, endocrine-disrupting, and immunomodulatory effects, its molecular mechanisms of toxicity remain incompletely understood, limiting mechanistically informed risk assessment. As evidence suggests that AOH acts as a multi-kinase inhibitor, this study aimed to expand its kinase target spectrum through integrated computational and experimental approaches. Ligand-based screening of structurally characterized kinase-ligand complexes, followed by molecular docking, molecular dynamics simulations, and free-energy calculations, identified phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) as a promising target. Functional validation was performed in Caco-2 and HT-29 human intestinal cells exposed to AOH (1-20 μM) for up to 5 h. PI3K activity was assessed by quantifying phosphorylation of its downstream effector Akt by Western blot, while AOH metabolism was characterized by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry. AOH induced a concentration-dependent reduction in phosphorylated Akt in Caco-2 cells at concentrations ≥ 10 μM without affecting total Akt, whereas no inhibition was observed in HT-29 cells. Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed decreased global protein phosphorylation in Caco-2 cells but increased phosphorylation in HT-29 cells. These contrasting responses were associated with differences in phase II metabolism, with extensive glucuronidation and sulfation occurring only in HT-29 cells. Computational analyses indicated that these metabolites exhibit reduced fitting into the ATP-binding pocket of PI3K. Overall, the findings identify PI3K as a novel molecular target of AOH and demonstrate that cellular metabolism critically determines its kinase-inhibitory activity.

articles.title: Additive hepatotoxicity of seneciphylline and lasiocarpine mixtures: multi-omics insights into P53 driven apoptosis and a Warburg-like metabolic reprogramming.
articles.abstract: Pyrrolizidine alkaloids (PAs) are widespread food contaminants whose co-occurrence poses serious yet poorly understood cumulative health risks. Here, using primary mouse hepatocytes and C57BL/6J mice combined with concentration addition (CA) and combination index (CI) models, we demonstrate that co-exposure to the prevalent 1,2-unsaturated PAs seneciphylline (Sp) and lasiocarpine (La) produces strictly additive hepatotoxicity across a wide concentration range (CI ≈ 1.0; 1/8 EC50 to 8 EC50). Mechanistically, combined exposure triggers mitochondrial calcium overload, ROS burst, and membrane potential collapse, leading to ultrastructural disintegration. Integrated targeted metabolomics and MitoCarta 3.0-based transcriptomics reveal a previously unappreciated Warburg-like metabolic reprogramming characterized by TCA cycle uncoupling, ATP depletion despite heightened cycle activity, and intracellular lactate acidosis driven by Pdk1-mediated pyruvate dehydrogenase inhibition and Slc16a3 downregulation. In vivo, co-exposure faithfully recapitulates human hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (HSOS) pathology, with additive activation of P53 target genes (Pmaip1, Hrk, Septin4) that dismantle anti-apoptotic BCL-2 defenses, culminating in cytochrome c release and caspase-9 cleavage. This multi-omics investigation establishes that additive hepatotoxicity of Sp and La arises from the convergence of two lethal cascades P53-driven mitochondrial apoptosis and metabolic energy catastrophe providing a mechanistic rationale for treating structurally related 1,2-unsaturated PAs as toxicological dose-surrogates in cumulative food safety risk assessment.

articles.title: Pharmacological correlates of topoisomerase II-directed protection against anthracycline-induced DNA damage and cardiotoxicity: a comparative evaluation of catalytic topoisomerase II inhibitors.
articles.abstract: Anthracyclines remain indispensable anticancer drugs, but their use is limited by dose-dependent cardiotoxicity involving topoisomerase IIβ (TOP2B)-mediated DNA damage in cardiomyocytes. To identify pharmacological features associated with TOP2-directed cardioprotection, we comparatively evaluated a chemically diverse panel of synthetic compounds, repurposed agents and natural products previously reported to modulate TOP2 activity, using dexrazoxane as the reference cardioprotectant. Recombinant human TOP2A and TOP2B inhibition was assessed by kDNA decatenation. Primary neonatal rat cardiomyocytes were pretreated with test compounds for 3 h and co-exposed to daunorubicin (DAU; 1.2 µM) for 3 h, followed by a 45-h drug-free period. TOP2 immunoreactivity was assessed after 24 h of compound exposure and DAU-induced γH2AX after 30-min pretreatment followed by 90-min DAU exposure. Effects on DAU antiproliferative activity were examined in HL-60 cells during 72-h exposure to 19 nM DAU. Dexrazoxane showed protective activity across the investigated endpoints. BNS-22 inhibited TOP2A and TOP2B with similar potency (IC₅₀ ≈ 2 µM for both isoforms) and produced the strongest protection among the experimental compounds, reducing DAU-induced LDH release by 55% at 10 µM, together with a 90% reduction in TOP2 immunoreactivity and 99.97% attenuation of DAU-induced γH2AX. BNS-22 did not attenuate DAU-induced antiproliferative activity in HL-60 cells. Resveratrol and suramin also provided significant protection at higher concentrations. Across this structurally diverse panel, biochemical TOP2 inhibition alone did not predict cardioprotection. Instead, protection was associated with a broader favourable cellular profile comprising low intrinsic toxicity, attenuation of anthracycline-induced DNA damage and, for the most effective compounds, reduced TOP2 immunoreactivity.

articles.title: Population-specific transcriptomic bioactivity assessment of perfluorooctanoic acid using human liver spheroids and physiologically based toxicokinetic modeling.
articles.abstract: Perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) has been widely used in industrial and consumer products and was recently classified as a Group 1 carcinogen by the International Agency for Research on Cancer. However, uncertainties remain regarding transcriptomic bioactivity thresholds associated with liver effects and their variability across clinically relevant populations. In this study, previously published transcriptomic data obtained following 24-h and 10-day exposure of primary human liver spheroids (LS) to PFOA were integrated into a physiologically based toxicokinetic (PBTK), population-specific framework to estimate transcriptomic human equivalent doses (HEDs). In addition, exploratory concordance analysis was performed between PFOA-responsive genes and liver hepatocellular carcinoma (LIHC)-associated transcriptomic profiles. Median transcriptomic HEDs ranged from 283 to 412 µg/kg body weight (bw)/week and were substantially higher than the estimated HEDs corresponding to the 95th percentile serum PFOA concentration in the U.S. population (0.0099 µg/kg bw/week) and the mean PFOA concentrations reported in human liver tissue samples (0.035 µg/kg bw/week). Obesity class III, cirrhosis Child-Pugh classes A and B, and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease reduced transcriptomic HEDs by approximately 31-41% compared with the healthy population, although HEDs remained substantially above reference values. Gene-level analysis identified only a limited number of genes within the bioactivity exposure ratio range of 1-100. More than 50% of PFOA-responsive genes exhibited concordant expression patterns with LIHC-associated transcriptomic profiles. Although the biological significance of these overlaps remains uncertain, concordance significantly exceeded that expected by chance from a background gene set and was driven mainly by down-regulated genes. Overall, this study provides a population-informed framework for integrating transcriptomic bioactivity data with PBTK modeling in human-relevant assessment of PFOA-associated liver effects.

articles.title: Gestational benzyl butyl phthalate exposure impairs sperm capacitation in F1 offspring by altering PKA-associated signaling and tyrosine phosphorylation.
articles.abstract: Benzyl butyl phthalate (BBP) is a phthalate plasticizer recognized as an endocrine-disrupting chemical. However, the effects of gestational BBP exposure on sperm function during capacitation in adult offspring remain unclear. This study investigated the effects of gestational BBP exposure on sperm function in adult male offspring, focusing on PKA-associated signaling and protein tyrosine phosphorylation. Pregnant ICR mice were orally administered BBP at 100, 250, or 500 mg/kg/day from gestational day 7 to 20.
