Adult male F1 offspring were evaluated on postnatal day 78, and sperm function was assessed by measuring motility, kinematic parameters, capacitation status, cell viability, intracellular ATP and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, PKA-associated signaling, and protein tyrosine phosphorylation. Gestational BBP exposure significantly reduced body weight, anogenital distance, and testicular size. While cell viability and intracellular ROS levels were unchanged, sperm motility and intracellular ATP levels were significantly reduced, capacitation status was altered, and the acrosome reaction was increased. Furthermore, PKA substrate phosphorylation and protein tyrosine phosphorylation were significantly decreased in spermatozoa. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that gestational BBP exposure impairs sperm function in adult male offspring, potentially through ATP depletion and disruption of capacitation-associated signaling pathways.

articles.title: Enantioselective disruption of human steroidogenesis in vitro by the azole fungicides imazalil, miconazole, and ketoconazole.
articles.abstract: Racemic mixtures of azoles such as imazalil, miconazole and ketoconazole are widely used as fungicides on food crops indirectly affecting humans or directly in humans as treatment of fungal infections. We investigated the potency of individual enantiomers (R- and S-imazalil, R- and S-miconazole and RS- and SR-ketoconazole), to disrupt human steroidogenesis in vitro. Effects of individual enantiomers and racemic mixtures on the canonical steroidogenic pathway were examined in the OECD standardized H295R steroidogenesis assay. Results indicate that disruption of steroidogenesis by the studied azoles is a highly enantioselective process, the degree of stereoselectivity being strongly dependent on the compound and the steroidogenic pathway. Results from the cell assay are supported by recombinant enzyme assays, where inhibition of CYP17A1-hydroxylase and -lyase as well as CYP19A1-aromatase activity was investigated. To shed light on the potential binding modes of the azoles, the enantiomers were also docked to CYP11A1, CYP17A1, CYP19A1 and CYP21A2 and selected poses subjected to molecular dynamics simulations, indicating differences in binding affinities but high potentials for endocrine disruption for all investigated enantiomers.

articles.title: Jintiange capsule as add-on therapy for lumbar disc herniation: an open-label randomized controlled trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Lumbar disc herniation (LDH) is a prevalent and costly disorder. Evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of Jintiange (JTG) capsules as add-on therapy for LDH remains limited. METHODS: This prospective, single-center, open-label randomized add-on trial compared JTG capsules plus conventional therapy with conventional therapy alone. The Japanese Orthopaedic Association (JOA) score was the sole primary outcome; VAS, SF-12 physical and mental component scores (PCS/MCS), numbness, lumbar muscle elastic modulus, and lumbar range of motion (ROM) were secondary outcomes. All 64 randomized participants were included according to their assigned groups. JOA, VAS, PCS, and MCS were analyzed using baseline-adjusted linear mixed-effects models incorporating all available post-baseline observations. Week 8 objective outcomes were analyzed using baseline-adjusted ANCOVA after multiple imputation. Multiplicity across the specified Week 8 secondary outcomes was controlled using the Holm procedure, and complete-case analyses were performed as sensitivity analyses. RESULTS: Seven participants discontinued follow-up (2 JTG, 5 control). The adjusted between-group difference in JOA favored the JTG-containing regimen at Week 2 (2.50 points, 95% CI 1.03-3.97; P < 0.001), Week 8 (2.73, 95% CI 1.21-4.26; P < 0.001), and 2-week follow-up (1.79, 95% CI 0.27-3.32; P = 0.021). At Week 8, adjusted differences also favored the JTG-containing regimen for VAS (-0.57, 95% CI -0.89 to -0.25), MCS (10.48, 95% CI 9.58-11.39), PCS (4.02, 95% CI 3.34-4.70), lumbar muscle elastic modulus (left -1.22, 95% CI -2.37 to -0.08; right -1.53, 95% CI -2.19 to -0.86), and ROM measures after multiplicity adjustment. Complete-case analyses showed similar effect directions. CONCLUSION: The JTG-containing regimen was associated with greater improvement in JOA and several secondary outcomes than conventional therapy alone. However, the open-label, non-placebo-controlled design, undocumented assessor blinding, differential attrition, multiplicity, small sample size, and single-center setting limit causal attribution and generalizability. Further blinded placebo-controlled multicenter trials are warranted. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://www.chictr.org.cn/, ChiCTR2300069735.

articles.title: Overcoming the efficacy-safety dilemma of cytokine therapy for tissue-resident memory T cells in cancer immunotherapy: Intrinsic sensitization and extrinsic optimization.
articles.abstract: Tissue-resident memory T (TRM) cells are important contributors to immune checkpoint blockade therapy response in several cancers, yet their therapeutic potential remains underutilized. The cytokine-mediated enhancement of TRM cells represents a promising strategy to amplify antitumor immunity. However, clinical translation is hindered by an efficacy-safety dilemma. Potent cytokines such as IL-12 and IL-15 induce severe systemic toxicity; other potent cytokines such as TGF-β and IL-1 carry inherent immunosuppressive risks. To overcome this barrier, a dual-strategy framework is proposed. Intrinsic sensitization involves the use of multidimensional regulatory networks such as those involving transcription factors, metabolic pathways, hypoxia signaling, and host aging to enhance TRM responsiveness to cytokines rather than increasing the dose. Complementing this, extrinsic optimization minimizes risks through targeted delivery systems, tumor microenvironment (TME) modulation for endogenous release, rational cytokine combination, and protein engineering coupled with rational selection. Collectively, this roadmap outlines how to harness cytokine networks safely and effectively, enabling precision TRM-based antitumor immunotherapy.

articles.title: Immunometabolic checkpoint: The dual regulatory role of macrophages in islet destruction in type 1 diabetes.
articles.abstract: Macrophage immunometabolic states are important determinants of inflammatory and reparative responses in type 1 diabetes (T1D). Within the diabetic islet, glycolysis, lipid metabolism, mitochondrial function, and metabolite-dependent epigenetic and post-translational mechanisms converge to regulate macrophage signaling, chromatin accessibility, and inflammatory output. M1-like/pro-inflammatory macrophages promote β-cell injury through nitric oxide and cytokine production, whereas M2-like/reparative states support efferocytosis, immune tolerance, and tissue homeostasis. These interconnected pathways form immunometabolic checkpoints that may be therapeutically targeted to reshape the islet immune microenvironment. Precision delivery strategies may further enable cell- and context-specific modulation while limiting systemic effects.

articles.title: Biochemistry of protozoan Metacaspases: Structure, processing, and inhibition.
articles.abstract: Metacaspases are calcium-dependent cysteine proteases (clan CD, family C14) present in fungi, protozoa, and plants but absent from mammals. Although structurally related to metazoan caspases, they differ in substrate specificity (cleaving after arginine or lysine), calcium-dependent activation, and monomeric architecture. In protozoan parasites such as Trypanosoma brucei, T. cruzi, Leishmania spp., Plasmodium spp., and Toxoplasma gondii, metacaspases regulate programmed cell death, cell cycle progression, protein quality control, differentiation, and virulence. Their absence in humans and essentiality in multiple parasitic life stages make them attractive drug targets for neglected tropical diseases. This review integrates structural, biochemical, functional, and pharmacological data on protozoan metacaspases. We examine calcium-dependent activation, the role of calcium homeostasis, functional diversification across parasite lineages, and the involvement of metacaspases in apoptotic and non-apoptotic pathways. Recent advances in small-molecule inhibitor discovery are covered, including oxime-based compounds, chalcones, flavonoids, peptidomimetics, and non-peptidyl scaffolds from virtual screening and rational design. A comparative biochemical analysis highlights species-specific differences in calcium dependence, processing, and regulation. Inhibitors are systematically classified by kinetic mechanism, offering a framework for understanding their mode of action and guiding structure-based drug design. We address selectivity challenges arising from metacaspase conservation across eukaryotes, distinguish experimentally validated binding sites from computationally predicted ones, and critically evaluate current in vivo and in vitro evidence for inhibitors in disease models. Finally, we discuss isoform redundancy, species-specific regulation, and translational development challenges, along with future research directions. Abreviations: YCA1, metacaspase deSaccharomyces cerevisiae; CaMCA-Ia, metacaspase deCandida albicans; TbMCA, metacaspase deTrypanosoma brucei; TcMCA, metacaspase deTrypanosoma cruzi; PCD, morte celular programada; TcoMCA5, metacaspase deTrypanosoma congolense; LmjMCA, metacaspase deLeishmania major; PfMCA, metacaspase de Plasmodium falciparum; TgMCA, metacaspase de Toxoplasma gondii; ADME, absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion; FRET, fluorescence resonance energy transfer; HAT, human African trypanosomiasis; IMC, inner membrane complex; MCA, metacaspase; PDB, Protein Data Bank; RNAi, RNA interference; TUNEL, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick end labeling.

articles.title: Towards rational carrier engineering: a review of interfacial binding, release mechanisms, and active delivery systems.
articles.abstract: Controlled release of active materials from carrier systems supports technologies spanning pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, cosmetics, and functional food products. Despite decades of research, the field remains fragmented: studies on physicochemical binding, release kinetics, and carrier architecture are often reported in isolation, making it difficult to translate mechanistic insight into analytical design rules. This review provides an integrated framework connecting the physicochemical interactions governing active-carrier binding. It illustrates the core mechanisms that dictate release (such as diffusion, swelling, degradation, and stimuli-triggered pathways). We also examine how carrier structural features modulate these mechanisms and ultimately determine release kinetics. We pay particular attention to the characterization techniques used to quantify release behavior, including in vitro testing methodologies, which remain a critical yet inconsistently standardized foundation for comparing carrier systems across studies. We also distinguish generalizable design principles from application-specific constraints, showing how carrier properties and release mechanisms translate across pharmaceutical, agrochemical, cosmetic, food, and environmental contexts.

articles.title: Cascade liposomal delivery for glioblastoma through multi-stage biological checkpoints.
articles.abstract: Although receptor-targeted liposomes provide promising opportunities for glioblastoma therapy, their clinical translation remains limited by sequential biological barriers encountered after systemic administration. Here, we establish a multi-stage checkpoint framework linking carrier properties with stage-specific transport constraints, including systemic clearance, BBB/BTB heterogeneity, extracellular matrix resistance, and myeloid sequestration. We analyze receptor-mediated transcytosis through a mechanistic triad of ligand engagement, intracellular sorting, and abluminal release, highlighting the binding-site barrier and affinity paradox that restrict effective parenchymal delivery. Successful transcytosis represents only the initial step and we further develop a cascade targeting framework integrating tissue penetration, tumor cell recognition, and intracellular payload availability. Key translational challenges, including tumor microenvironment modulation, Quality by Design (QbD) manufacturing, safety, and companion diagnostics, are critically examined. Future progress will depend on evaluating liposomal platforms according to productive cellular exposure, with bulk accumulation serving only as a supporting measure, and on using quantitative transport profiling and imaging-guided stratification to identify patients whose biological barriers are compatible with specific liposomal designs.

articles.title: Non-viral delivery and genome editing for CAR-NK engineering in solid tumors: from ex vivo manufacturing to in vivo reprogramming.
articles.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered natural killer (NK) cell therapy has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer treatment, offering advantages over CAR-T cells such as a lower risk of cytokine release syndrome and graft-versus-host disease and the potential for off-the-shelf manufacturing. Viral vectors have long served as effective tools for CAR-NK engineering, but their dependence on complex manufacturing procedures, considerable production costs, and the potential risks associated with genomic integration has encouraged increasing interest in non-viral alternatives. Recent advances in genetic engineering technologies have facilitated the development of CAR-NK platforms, particularly through non-viral delivery approaches including electroporation, transposon systems and lipid nanoparticles, while CRISPR-based tools enable targeted genome editing. Meanwhile, an increasing number of clinical trials have begun to evaluate the safety and therapeutic potential of CAR-NK cells in both hematological malignancies and solid tumors. However, challenges such as limited NK-cell persistence, antigen heterogeneity, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment remain. In this review, we summarize recent progress in non-viral CAR-NK engineering strategies, analyze the current landscape of preclinical and clinical trials, and discuss key challenges and future directions for advancing CAR-NK therapy. Collectively, these advances suggest that non-viral engineering technologies may serve as an important technological foundation for next-generation CAR-NK therapies, enabling more flexible ex vivo manufacturing and potentially supporting the future development of in vivo CAR-NK generation strategies for solid tumors.

articles.title: Safety and drug-drug interaction profiles of Oral selective estrogen receptor degraders: implications for clinical practice.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Oral selective estrogen receptor degraders (SERDs) have transformed the treatment landscape for patients with hormone receptor-positive, HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer harboring ESR1 mutations. As their use expands, understanding their pharmacokinetic properties, safety profiles, and drug-drug interaction (DDI) potential is essential, particularly in patients with hepatic impairment, comorbidities, and polypharmacy. AREAS COVERED: This review summarizes current evidence on the pharmacokinetics, metabolism, safety, dose modification strategies, and clinically relevant DDIs of the two FDA-approved oral SERDs, elacestrant and imlunestrant. Practical considerations regarding CYP3A4-mediated interactions, transporter-related DDIs, hepatic and renal impairment, and concomitant medication management are discussed. EXPERT OPINION: Oral SERDs demonstrate favorable safety profiles and substantially lower DDI burdens than CDK4/6 inhibitors, facilitating their integration into routine clinical practice. Elacestrant is more susceptible to CYP3A4-mediated interactions, whereas imlunestrant exhibits a lower interaction burden owing to its multiple metabolic pathways. Careful assessment of concomitant medications and hepatic function remains essential to optimize treatment efficacy and minimize toxicity. As clinical experience grows, a deeper understanding of the pharmacological characteristics of oral SERDs will further support individualized endocrine therapy for metastatic breast cancer.

articles.title: Therapeutic potential of Boswellia-derived compounds in skin conditions.
articles.abstract: Boswellia species and the resins like frankincense derived from them have long been used in traditional medical systems for the treatment of inflammatory and skin disorders owing to their diverse bioactive constituents. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the dermatological potential of Boswellia species and their metabolites in inflammatory and non-inflammatory skin diseases, with particular emphasis on boswellic acids. A PRISMA-guided literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and ScienceDirect identified studies on the phytochemistry, biological activities, and dermatological applications of frankincense-producing species, supplemented by information on taxonomy and traditional uses. The genus Boswellia comprises more than 20 recognized species distributed across the Indian subcontinent, the Arabian Peninsula, and the Horn of Africa. Their oleo-gum resins are rich in pentacyclic triterpenes, particularly 11-keto-β-boswellic acid (KBA) and 3-O-acetyl-11-keto-β-boswellic acid (AKBA), which exert anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, antimicrobial, immunomodulatory, and wound-healing activities. Preclinical studies demonstrate that Boswellia-derived preparations attenuate key pathogenic pathways in psoriasis, eczema, and atopic dermatitis, promote wound healing, and protect against radiation and burn-induced skin injury. Emerging evidence also supports potential applications in skin aging, pigmentation disorders, and melanoma. Clinical studies suggest that topical Boswellia formulations may improve psoriasis, eczema, photoaging, striae distensae, and radiotherapy induced skin reactions; however, the available evidence is limited by small sample sizes, short treatment durations, heterogeneous methodologies, and variability in species, extraction procedures, and formulations. Overall, Boswellia species, particularly B. sacra, B. serrata, B. papyrifera, and B. carterii, represent promising multi-target candidates for dermatological applications. Future research should prioritize sustainable sourcing, phytochemical standardization, species-specific comparisons, and well-designed clinical trials to establish efficacy, optimal formulations, dosing strategies, and long-term safety.

articles.title: Dickkopf-3 (DKK3) in cardiovascular diseases: from a stress-responsive biomarker to a potential therapeutic target.
articles.abstract: Dickkopf-3 (DKK3) is a secreted glycoprotein that functions as a context-dependent modulator of the Wnt/β-catenin and transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling pathways. Originally studied in development and cancer, DKK3 has recently emerged as a key stress-responsive factor. It is released by epithelial and other cell types under pathological strain and actively participates in fibrotic, inflammatory, and remodeling processes across various organ systems. In cardiovascular medicine, DKK3 is gaining recognition not only as a promising biomarker for renal and vascular injury-conditions closely intertwined with cardiovascular outcomes-but also as a direct mediator in the pathogenesis of specific cardiovascular conditions such as abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) and heart failure. This review synthesizes current knowledge on DKK3, beginning with its fundamental biology and established roles in renal, pulmonary, and dermal fibrosis, which provide crucial mechanistic parallels. We then focus on the evolving evidence of DKK3's involvement in cardiovascular diseases, critically evaluating its biomarker potential for risk stratification in conditions like diabetic kidney disease and its direct pathophysiological roles in vascular smooth muscle cell phenotype switching, myocardial remodeling, and aneurysm formation. We delve into specific molecular mechanisms, including interactions with the ATF6-TGFβ3-Smad2/3 axis and low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1), as revealed by preclinical models. Finally, we explore the therapeutic implications of targeting the DKK3 axis, discuss the challenges posed by its context-dependent dual roles, and outline future research directions necessary to translate these discoveries into clinical applications for cardiovascular patients.

articles.title: Curcumin in solid organ transplantation: current evidence, mechanisms, and translational challenges.
articles.abstract: Solid organ transplantation faces complex pathophysiological challenges, including ischemia-reperfusion injury (IRI), alloimmune rejection, and chronic graft dysfunction. These interconnected processes involve multiple signaling pathways, yet these complex interconnected pathological processes remain a significant clinical challenge. In contrast, natural plant-derived compounds often possess pleiotropic pharmacological activities and may offer a multi-targeted approach to modulate the overall pathological milieu. Curcumin, a representative bioactive natural polyphenol from Curcuma longa, exhibits potent antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and immunomodulatory properties and has shown therapeutic benefits across a wide range of diseases. In the context of transplantation, preliminary studies have demonstrated encouraging effects in improving graft preservation, attenuating injury, and modulating immune response. However, direct investigation of curcumin in solid organ transplantation remains limited, with fragmented evidence and a weak foundational basis. This review aims to systematically synthesize the current evidence for curcumin's application in kidney, liver, heart, and lung transplantation, to assess the translational hurdles, and to propose a strategic roadmap for future research. We also propose a mechanistic framework for curcumin's potential actions based on established studies in related fields, including IRI, inflammatory diseases, and immunology, intended to generate testable hypotheses for future transplant-focused research. By identifying key knowledge gaps and highlighting promising mechanistic pathways, we hope to stimulate further investigation and accelerate the clinical translation of this pleiotropic natural compound into transplant medicine.

articles.title: Renal anemia: from erythropoietin deficiency to erythropoietin resistance.
articles.abstract: Renal anemia is one of the core complications of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and is closely associated with poor patient prognosis. Renal interstitial fibrosis or impaired oxygen sensing leads to insufficient erythropoietin (EPO) production, which constitutes the fundamental mechanism initiating renal anemia. On this basis, multiple pathological factors-including the inflammatory microenvironment in CKD, iron deficiency, and mineral and bone disorders-synergistically induce EPO resistance, further exacerbating anemia and diminishing the response to existing therapies. Currently, the treatment of renal anemia has moved beyond simple EPO replacement and is progressively shifting toward a dual strategy that emphasizes both correction of EPO resistance and enhancement of drug responsiveness. This article summarizes the molecular network through which insufficient EPO synthesis and EPO resistance synergistically aggravate renal anemia, systematically reviews the pharmacological basis, limitations, and safety risks of current drug therapies, and discusses future research directions and potential therapeutic targets in this field.

articles.title: Chinese herbal medicine for ulcerative colitis: product-level clinical evidence, mechanistic appraisal, and a roadmap to precision translation.
articles.abstract: Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) is widely used for ulcerative colitis (UC), but product heterogeneity, variable trial quality, and limited long-term safety data preclude class-level efficacy claims. This critical narrative review therefore evaluates evidence at the level of the defined botanical drug product, formulation, route, dose, and manufacturing process. The review focuses on traditional formulas, processed botanical drugs, and proprietary preparations with documented use in Chinese medical practice. Purified plant metabolites such as curcumin and common flavonoids are not treated as uniquely Chinese interventions; they are discussed only when they are part of a defined CHM-related product or when pivotal natural-product trials provide a relevant product-level comparator. Primary randomized trials show heterogeneous results: higher-dose curcumin trials and the curcumin-QingDai combination provide signals of benefit, low-dose curcumin was negative, and indigo naturalis shows dose-related efficacy accompanied by important safety concerns. Mechanistically, the strongest evidence comes from human target engagement or causal perturbation, exemplified by mucosal CYP1A1 induction with curcumin-QingDai and loss of indigo naturalis efficacy in Ahr-deficient mice. Most other mechanistic claims remain preclinical and model-dependent. Translation requires taxonomically authenticated and chemically characterized products, measured exposure, causal mechanism testing, objective CORE-IBD/STRIDE-II-aligned outcomes, CONSORT-CHM reporting, and prospective, batch-traceable pharmacovigilance. No molecular, microbial, or traditional-pattern biomarker has yet shown a prospectively validated treatment-by-biomarker interaction for a defined CHM product. Precision translation should therefore be regarded as a prospective research program rather than an achieved clinical state.

articles.title: Cellular senescence in ovarian cancer: a proposed geroncogenic shift linking aging, plasticity, and therapy resistance.
articles.abstract: Ovarian cancer develops within a biological environment that changes substantially with age. Beyond chronological aging, progressive alterations in genome maintenance, telomere integrity, epigenetic regulation, mitochondrial function, metabolism, inflammation, and immune surveillance can reshape the cellular and tissue context in which tumor evolution occurs. Cellular senescence represents a critical point of convergence within this process. Although senescence can restrict the proliferation of damaged or oncogenically stressed cells, persistent senescent cells remain metabolically active and can alter their surroundings through the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). Here, we propose the concept of a geroncogenic shift to describe how age-associated changes in tissue homeostasis may create stress-response states that are subsequently exploited by malignant and stromal cells. We distinguish two named, complementary components of the framework: systemic decline, referring to the progressive deterioration of cellular and tissue homeostasis during aging, and pathway-specific hijacking, referring to the selective co-option of altered stress-response pathways under oncogenic or therapeutic pressure. Cellular senescence provides a functional interface between these processes because the same stress responses that constrain damaged cells can, when persistent or incompletely resolved, contribute to tumor adaptation. In ovarian cancer, senescence is not a uniform cellular endpoint. Its consequences vary according to the initiating stress, cellular compartment, molecular program, duration, and capacity for recovery or escape. Tumor-cell senescence may suppress proliferation yet also be associated with stem-like adaptation and therapeutic persistence. Senescence-associated changes in fibroblasts and other stromal populations can reshape inflammatory signaling and treatment response, while polyploid and senescence-like states illustrate the extent of cellular plasticity that can exist after therapeutic stress. The SASP further extends the effects of senescence beyond individual cells by influencing neighboring tumor and stromal populations, extracellular-matrix remodeling, inflammation, and dissemination. This perspective has important therapeutic implications. Rather than treating senescence as either a uniformly protective or pathogenic state, therapeutic strategies should distinguish between senescent-cell elimination, SASP modulation, metabolic vulnerabilities, and prevention of senescence escape. We propose that understanding the cellular context and temporal dynamics of senescence will be essential for determining when senescence should be induced, maintained, modulated, or eliminated in ovarian cancer. Most therapeutic evidence for senescence-directed strategies remains preclinical, and clinical translation will require cell-type-specific biomarkers and optimized treatment timing. The geroncogenic shift framework therefore provides a conceptual basis for linking aging biology with tumor evolution and for developing more selective approaches to senescence-directed therapy.

articles.title: Pharmacological regulation of chondrocyte ferroptosis by plant-derived metabolites in osteoarthritis: from molecular mechanisms to targeted nanodelivery.
articles.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) lacks approved disease-modifying pharmacotherapy. Chondrocyte ferroptosis-iron-dependent phospholipid peroxidation caused by disrupted iron handling, lipid metabolism, and antioxidant defense-has been implicated in cartilage degeneration and is pharmacologically suppressible in experimental models. Natural products can modulate multiple ferroptosis-related nodes, including the Nrf2/SLC7A11/GPX4 axis, ACSL4-dependent lipid peroxidation, iron homeostasis, and mitochondrial redox balance. Their translation, however, is limited by poor solubility, instability, rapid clearance, uncertain dose-exposure relationships, and restricted cartilage penetration. This review integrates the pharmacological basis of chondrocyte ferroptosis, evidence for anti-ferroptotic natural products, and nanodelivery strategies that improve joint retention, cartilage targeting, chondrocyte uptake, and controlled release. We distinguish direct ferroptosis evidence from adjacent antioxidant or chondroprotective findings and evaluate polymeric, lipid-based, hydrogel, biomimetic, inorganic, and hybrid platforms as pharmacological optimization tools. Current integrated systems show encouraging structure-preserving effects in experimental OA, but evidence remains predominantly preclinical. Translation will require standardized compounds, ferroptosis-specific target-engagement assays, pharmacokinetic and dose-response studies, carrier-specific safety testing, clinically relevant models, and biomarker-guided patient selection. Rationally matching natural-product pharmacology with joint-specific delivery may enable mechanism-based OA therapies.

articles.title: Gut microbiota-immune-bone axis in osteoporosis: mechanisms and intervention strategies.
articles.abstract: Osteoporosis (OP) remains a major global health burden, yet current pharmacological interventions are constrained by adverse effects, limited efficacy, and a bone-centric therapeutic paradigm that overlooks upstream pathogenic drivers. Emerging evidence positions the gut microbiota (GM) as a critical rheostat of bone homeostasis, operating through a gut-immune-bone axis that integrates microbial metabolism, intestinal barrier integrity, and systemic immune regulation. This review systematically examines the immunopathological mechanisms of OP, with particular emphasis on the GM-derived metabolites-short-chain fatty acids, secondary bile acids, tryptophan derivatives, lipopolysaccharide, and trimethylamine N-oxide-that orchestrate osteoclastogenic versus osteoprotective outcomes via key immune checkpoints including the Th17/Treg, macrophage phenotypic polarization, and regulatory B cell axes. We further delineate the subtype-specific heterogeneity of this axis across postmenopausal, senile, glucocorticoid-induced, and diabetic osteoporosis, highlighting distinct microbial and immune signatures that mandate stratified therapeutic approaches. Importantly, we evaluate the translational potential of GM-targeted interventions-probiotics, prebiotics, fecal microbiota transplantation, and dietary modulation-as adjunctive or standalone strategies, and discuss their synergistic interplay with conventional anti-osteoporotic agents. By reframing OP as a systems-level disorder of the gut-immune-bone circuitry, this review establishes a mechanistic groundwork for precision medicine, identifies novel druggable targets, and charts a course toward safer, more durable, and disease-modifying anti-osteoporotic therapies.

articles.title: Microbiota-host crosstalk in ulcerative colitis: mechanistic evidence and translational prospects for traditional Chinese medicine.
articles.abstract: Ulcerative colitis (UC) is sustained by reciprocal interactions among intestinal dysbiosis, altered microbial metabolism, epithelial barrier dysfunction, and mucosal immune activation. This narrative review examines that microbiota-metabolism-barrier-immune network and evaluates how traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) may influence it. Human multi-omics studies indicate that UC-associated dysbiosis is more reproducible at the level of microbial function and metabolite output than at the level of individual taxa. Experimental studies further implicate short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, tryptophan-derived indoles, arginine, and choline-related metabolites in epithelial and immune regulation. Most evidence for TCM-mediated microbiota modulation, however, comes from chemically induced experimental colitis, organoid, or cell systems; human interventional evidence remains limited. We therefore grade mechanistic evidence from association through microbiota dependence, candidate strain/metabolite sufficiency, host-target validation, and integrated causal-chain validation. This distinction avoids treating genus-level relative-abundance changes as proof of microbial benefit or mediation. Emerging clinical trials of indigo naturalis, Curcumin-QingDai, Andrographis paniculata extract, curcumin, and selected multicomponent Chinese herbal therapies provide short-term efficacy signals, but results are preparation- and dose-dependent and do not yet establish microbiota-mediated clinical efficacy. Translation will require chemically standardized products, rigorous safety surveillance, strain- and function-resolved microbiome measurements, explicit experiments separating direct herbal actions from microbiota-dependent effects, and clinical trials incorporating endoscopic, histological, pharmacokinetic, microbial, metabolic, and long-term safety outcomes.

articles.title: Phytogenic zinc oxide nanoparticles in breast cancer therapy: an ethnopharmacological perspective on multi-targeted mechanistic pathways and translational constraints.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Breast cancer remains the most frequently diagnosed malignancy and the leading cause of cancer death among women worldwide as of 2026. While conventional interventions face challenges like drug resistance and systemic toxicity, the integration of green nanotechnology with ethnopharmacology offers a biocompatible, sustainable alternative. This review assesses the mechanistic pathways and therapeutic potential of phytogenic zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) synthesized using bioactive secondary metabolites. METHODS: This review combines findings from nine recent studies exploring biogenic ZnO NPs derived from diverse biological sources, including Rhus coriaria L. (Anacardiaceae), Withania somnifera (L.) Dunal (Solanaceae), Zingiber officinale Roscoe (Zingiberaceae). We critically analysed the characterization parameters, synthesis methods and pharmacological efficacy across 3D architectural spheroids, 2D monolayer cultures, and select in vivo models. RESULTS: The collective data demonstrate that biogenic ZnO-NPs induce potent apoptosis through BAX upregulation, ROS-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction and specific cell cycle arrest. Notable benchmarks include tumour suppression comparable to Tamoxifen in in vivo models using melon-derived extracts and an IC50 of 14.7 μg/mL in 3D MCF-7 spheroids for ginger-mediated NPs. DISCUSSION: In spite of the promising results, a critical methodological tension exists between limited preclinical validation and innovative synthesis. The pervasive reliance on 2D models often fails to duplicate the dense architectural barriers of solid tumours. Future research must prioritize a realistic translational pathway, shifting from basic in vitro models to rigorous in vivo biodistribution profiling, detailed metabolic tracking, and long-term toxicological assessments against normal mammary epithelial controls (e.g., MCF-10A) to actually establish, rather than merely hypothesize, a definitive, selective therapeutic index and ensure baseline physiological safety.

articles.title: NRF2 modulation in colorectal cancer chemoprevention: integrating traditional medicine with translational strategies against oxidative stress, inflammation, and cancer stem cells.
articles.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is an important and significant reason for cancer-related morbidity and mortality globally. Treatment remains challenging due to recurrence, metastasis, and chemoresistance. Evidence shows that oxidative stress, ongoing inflammation, and cancer stem cells (CSCs) play essential functions in CRC development and progression. Nrf2 is a master regulator of cellular redox balance through the Keap1-Nrf2-is signalling pathway. Normal activation of Nrf2 protects colonic cells from oxidative DNA harm and inflammation during initial carcinogenesis. However, sustained Nrf2 activation in tumours encourages chemoresistance, metabolic reprogramming, and CSC upkeep, showing a dual role. Traditional medicine and dietary phytochemicals (curcumin, sulforaphane, resveratrol, EGCG, berberine) can modulate Nrf2 while interacting with NF-κB, Wnt/β-catenin, and Notch pathways. This review synthesises mechanistic and translational evidence on Nrf2 modulation in CRC chemoprevention, stressing conventional medicine-derived agents in modern approaches. It moreover highlights difficulties, limitations, and future viewpoints for precision chemoprevention and personalised interventions.

articles.title: Hazard identification was the aim: reply to Zhao et al. on the exposure context of flavoured-air inhaler toxicity.
Structural context matters when interpreting clozapine AHR docking.
Interleukin-17D Deficiency Attenuates Atherosclerosis by Diminishing Macrophage Inflammation and Promoting M2 Phenotype.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Macrophages are central to atherosclerosis by driving vascular inflammation, plaque growth, and instability. Although interleukin-17D (IL-17D) has been linked to endothelial inflammation, its role in macrophage-mediated atherosclerosis remains unclear. OBJECTIVES: This study investigated the function and mechanism of macrophage IL-17D in atherosclerosis. METHODS: Using IL-17D knockout, macrophage-specific IL-17D knockdown, and macrophage-specific Spi-B knockdown mouse models on an ApoE-/- background, we assessed aortic lesion burden, necrotic core formation, macrophage accumulation, inflammatory responses, and macrophage polarization. Mechanistic studies were performed using transcriptomic analysis, ChIP-PCR, and luciferase reporter assays. RESULTS: IL-17D deficiency markedly reduced atherosclerotic plaque formation in the whole aorta and aortic root, decreased necrotic core size, and limited macrophage accumulation and vascular inflammation. Both in vitro and in vivo, IL-17D deficiency promoted M2 macrophage polarization while suppressing pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. Macrophage-specific IL-17D knockdown similarly attenuated atherosclerotic lesion development and inflammation. Mechanistically, IL-17D deficiency activated the Spi-B-STAT6 transcriptional axis. Macrophage-specific Spi-B knockdown reversed the anti-atherosclerotic effects of IL-17D deficiency, confirming its functional importance. Rosuvastatin suppressed IL-17D expression, and IL-17D repression contributed to its anti-inflammatory and anti-atherogenic effects. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify macrophage-derived IL-17D as a key regulator of atherosclerosis. Targeting IL-17D may promote protective M2 polarization and alleviate vascular inflammation, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for atherosclerotic disease.

articles.title: A machine learning-based model for predicting the color of liquid formulation placebos and analyzing their visual similarity.
articles.abstract: High-quality randomized, placebo-controlled trials are critical for clinical drug trials, but preparing color‑matched placebos for liquid formulations remains difficult due to the color complexity of liquid formulations and the inefficiency of conventional matching methods. Machine learning offers an effective approach to modeling the complex non-linear relationships among multiple colorants at varying concentrations, enabling prediction of color formulations. This study employed optimal Latin hypercube sampling to generate 253 simulated samples with five colorants. After color correction using a correction matrix, ten color space values were extracted for model fitting. Among five models, random forest (RF) performed best, with a mean absolute error of 0.09, a root mean square error of 0.15, and an R2 value of 0.69. Shapley additive explanations analysis identified L*, G, gray, and V as key variables influencing the prediction of placebo color formulations. Validation against eight target solutions produced average color differences of ΔEab = 3.35 and ΔE00 = 2.20, and a mean visual similarity score of 9.1 by human assessors, indicating a relatively high prediction accuracy. This study developed an RF‑based strategy for predicting the color of placebo in liquid formulations, enabling visual color matching with test drugs in clinical trials.

articles.title: Bovine serum Albumin-Mediated effects on colonic Solubility, mucus Permeation, and absorption of celecoxib.
articles.abstract: Celecoxib was used as a model compound in fasted state simulated colonic fluid (FaSSCoF) to investigate equilibrium drug solubility (Seq), protein binding using rapid equilibrium dialysis (RED), flux and permeability (Papp) across porcine colonic mucus (PCM), and in vivo colonic absorption using a rat intracolonic instillation model. The primary focus was on the role of bovine serum albumin (BSA) as a solubilizing and binding constituent, while bile salts (sodium taurodeoxycholate, TDC) with lecithin and poloxamer 407 were included as comparative systems to evaluate how differences in solubilizer type influence celecoxib permeability and absorption. BSA demonstrated a pronounced solubilizing effect on celecoxib with a 1:1 M binding ratio, increasing the apparent Seq from 5.1 µg/mL to 92 µg/mL in FaSSCoF containing 15 mg/mL BSA. Under these conditions, diffusion across PCM increased approximately seven-fold compared with FaSSCoF without BSA, accompanied by a four-fold increase in colonic absorption in vivo. In contrast, when celecoxib concentration was maintained constant and BSA was subsequently added to FaSSCoF, diffusion across PCM decreased up to ten-fold at BSA concentrations of 1.5 mg/mL, accompanied by an approximately 30 % decrease in colonic absorption in vivo. This behavior is consistent with an increased BSA-bound fraction and a reduced free drug concentration available for transport. The addition of TDC with lecithin or poloxamer 407 similarly increased celecoxib diffusion across PCM and colonic absorption when celecoxib was dissolved at Seq in FaSSCoF, although no statistically significant differences were observed between the solubilizing systems. Overall, these findings demonstrate that solubilizing constituents in colonic fluids can substantially increase drug solubility, mucus permeation, and colonic absorption, highlighting the importance of accounting for protein-drug interactions when evaluating drug behavior in the colon.

articles.title: Minthostachys verticillata aqueous extract ameliorates intestinal and systemic alterations induced by a model of acute stress.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGIC RELEVANCE: Minthostachys verticillata (Griseb.) Epling (Lamiaceae), popularly known as Peperina (Mv), is a native plant widely used in traditional medicine as a digestive, sedative, antispasmodic, antidiarrheal, antiemetic, and carminative agent. However, its potential beneficial effects on intestinal and systemic changes induced by acute stress have not been fully elucidated. AIM OF THE STUDY: To assess the effects of its aqueous extract on the gastrointestinal system in a rat model of acute restraint stress related to inflammatory intestinal pathologies. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Animals were treated for four consecutive days (n=6 per group) with Mv extract (250 and 500 mg/Kg p.o), clonazepam (1 mg/Kg p.o) or water. The acute stress model was induced by restraint for 6 hours in plastic cones adapted to the animal one hour after the last dose of the treatments. Control animals were not subjected to stress. Following the restraint period, animals were removed from the plastic cone and weighed. Glycemia and corticosterone were determined in plasma. Histological analysis and inflammatory and permeability markers were measured in colon and ileum samples. RESULTS: Stressed animals exhibited elevated corticosterone levels and intestinal damage, including villous rupture, goblet cell depletion, and increased biogenic amines levels. Treatment with Mv extract prevented these alterations in the ileum and colon and improved short-chain fatty acid profiles, especially butyrate and acetate in the colon. Stress also increased the glutathione redox ratio, upregulated inflammatory markers (TNFα, IL-1β, IL-6, TGFβ) and PI3K/AKT pathway proteins in the colon, effects that were attenuated by the extract. Furthermore, markers associated with cytoskeletal uncoupling (pVASP) and extracellular matrix remodeling (MMP-2) were reduced by Mv, suggesting a protective effect against stress-induced mucosal structural and molecular alterations. No changes were observed in myeloperoxidase activity, indicating that neutrophils were likely not involved in the observed inflammatory response. CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates, for the first time, the ability of Mv to reduce the imbalance induced by acute restraint stress. Mitigation of inflammatory cascades, preservation of goblet cell lineage, attenuation of markers associated with cytoskeletal uncoupling (pVASP) and extracellular matrix remodeling (MMP-2) markers, and maintenance of colonic short-chain fatty acids represent key protective mechanisms. These findings suggest that Mv could exert beneficial effects in stress-related intestinal disorders.

articles.title: Artepillin C from Artemisia capillaris attenuates liver fibrosis by targeting NR3C2 and regulating the PPAR-γ/Smad axis.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Artemisia capillaris is a traditional Chinese medicinal herb and widely used for the treatment of jaundice, hepatitis, and other liver-related diseases. Contemporary pharmacological studies have revealed its hepatoprotective, anti-inflammatory, and anti-fibrotic activities. However, the bioactive constituents responsible for its anti-hepatic fibrotic effect remain poorly defined. Artepillin C (AC), one of the coumaric acid derivatives isolated from A. capillaris, has not yet been studied in liver fibrosis, and its mechanism of action is still unknown. AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to evaluate the anti-hepatic fibrotic effects of AC in vitro and in vivo, and to elucidate its molecular target and underlying mechanism. MATERIALS AND METHODS: The anti-fibrotic activity of AC was assessed in transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1)-induced hepatic stellate cell (HSC) activation models using LX-2 and JS-1 cells, and validated in a carbon tetrachloride (CCl4)-induced mouse model of liver fibrosis. The expression of extracellular matrix (ECM)-related markers were analyzed by Western blot, RT-qPCR, and immunofluorescence (IF). Transcriptomic analysis, target prediction and experimental screening were introduced to identify potential molecular targets of AC. The interaction between AC and target was validated by molecular docking and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, which were supported by the cellular thermal shift assay (CETSA) and drug affinity responsive target stability (DARTS). Receptor agonist/antagonist treatment, and co-immunoprecipitation (Co-IP) were conducted to explore the anti-fibrotic mechanism of AC. RESULTS: AC markedly attenuated TGF-β1-induced activation of HSCs without apparent cytotoxicity and reduced the expression of ECM proteins, including fibronectin (FN) and collagen I. In CCl4-induced mice, AC alleviated liver injury and reduced ECM deposition. Transcriptomic analysis combined with target prediction suggested that nuclear receptor subfamily 3 group C member 2 (NR3C2) was a potential target of AC. Docking and MD simulation indicated that AC could interact with NR3C2, while the CETSA and DARTS further demonstrated that AC binds to NR3C2 and increases its resistance to thermal denaturation and protease digestion. Mechanistically, AC downregulated NR3C2 expression, weakened the interaction between NR3C2 and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor-γ (PPAR-γ), and restored PPAR-γ levels at higher concentrations, thereby suppressing TGF-β1-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation. Consistent with these results, activation of NR3C2 enhanced Smad2/3 phosphorylation, whereas inhibition of NR3C2 or PPAR-γ attenuated Smad2/3 phosphorylation. CONCLUSION: This study suggests that AC, a natural product derived from A. capillaris, attenuates liver fibrosis by targeting NR3C2 and regulating the PPAR-γ/Smad axis. These findings provide mechanistic insight into the anti-fibrotic effects of AC and further expand the pharmacological understanding of A. capillaris-derived bioactive constituents.

articles.title: Changma Xifeng Tablet alleviates Tourette syndrome by restoring striatal dopaminergic homeostasis via the C1qa/TLR4-mediated microglial polarization.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: The traditional botanical formulation Changma Xifeng (CMXF), primarily composed of the rhizomes of Gastrodia elata Blume and the roots of Paeonia lactiflora Pall., has been historically utilized in ethnomedicine to treat involuntary muscle spasms and hyperactive motor anomalies. It has shown therapeutic potential in preclinical models of Tourette syndrome (TS). AIM OF THE STUDY: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of Changma Xifeng Tablet (CMXF) in a 3,3-iminodipropionitrile (IDPN)-induced Tourette syndrome-like rat model and to explore whether C1qa-associated neuroimmune changes are associated with CMXF treatment. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Male Sprague-Dawley rats were intraperitoneally injected with IDPN (350 mg/kg/day) for 7 consecutive days to establish a TS model. Rats were randomly divided into seven groups (n = 10 each): Control, CMXF-only, TS model, CMXF-L (78 mg/kg), CMXF-M (156 mg/kg), CMXF-H (312 mg/kg), and Tiapride (21 mg/kg). CMXF was administered orally once daily for 4 weeks. Behavioral assessments (stereotyped scores), histopathology (H&E and Nissl), striatal proteomics, Western blot, ELISA, and immunofluorescence were performed to evaluate therapeutic effects and mechanisms. RESULTS: CMXF significantly ameliorated tic-like stereotyped behaviors, reducing stereotyped scores by 51% versus the TS group (p < 0.001), and improved monoamine disturbances in TS rats. Specifically, compared with the Control group, TS rats exhibited increased striatal DA and NE levels (70.4 vs. 33.9 and 0.589 vs. 0.208, respectively), together with decreased brainstem 5-HT and striatal HVA levels (4.57 vs. 10.7 and 16.84 vs. 24.14, respectively), whereas CMXF-H markedly reversed these abnormalities, reducing striatal DA and NE to 39.3 and 0.288 and increasing brainstem 5-HT and striatal HVA to 8.81 and 24.34, respectively. CMXF-H also attenuated TS-associated alterations in striatal dopamine-related signaling, reducing the elevated expression of DRD1 and DRD2 by 61% and 15%, respectively, while increasing the reduced expression of COMT and MAO-B by 43% and 46%, respectively (p < 0.05 or p < 0.01). Proteomic profiling highlighted the classical complement cascade as a candidate pathway associated with CMXF treatment. Further analyses showed that CMXF treatment was associated with a 20% reduction in C1qa upregulation and decreased C1qa deposition on activated microglia (p < 0.05). CMXF treatment was also associated with attenuation of the TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB signaling pathway and changes in microglia-associated markers, characterized by a 30% decrease in iNOS and a 47% increase in Arg-1 (p < 0.01). These changes coincided with reduced striatal neuroinflammation, with TNF-α and IL-1β decreasing by 21% and 46%, respectively (p < 0.01 or p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies C1qa-associated neuroinflammatory changes as a molecular feature of the IDPN-induced TS-like rat model and a candidate pathway associated with CMXF treatment. CMXF treatment was associated with reduced C1qa expression, attenuation of TLR4/MyD88/NF-κB-related signaling, changes in M1/M2-associated microglial markers, and improvement in monoamine-related alterations. These findings suggest a potential relationship between C1qa-associated neuroinflammatory changes and the pharmacological effects of CMXF, while the causal role of C1qa remains to be determined.

articles.title: Da Chuanxiong extract modulates the Lands cycle to elicit spatially specific phospholipid remodeling against cerebral ischemia.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Da Chuanxiong (DCX), composed of Ligusticum chuanxiong Hort. and Gastrodia elata Bl. (4:1), is a classical Chinese herbal formula, traditionally used for headache and vertigo caused by wind pathogen and blood stasis. Modern clinical practice has extended its application to ischemic stroke. However, whether DCX exerts neuroprotection through Lands cycle-mediated phospholipid remodeling, particularly in a spatially specific manner, remains unclear. AIM OF THE STUDY: To demonstrate whether DCX elicits spatially specific phospholipid remodeling through Lands cycle activation, and to identify the brain-penetrating constituents responsible for this effect. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Protective effects of DCX were evaluated in pMCAO rats, and those of its brain-penetrating constituents were assessed in OGD/R-induced HT22 cells. Glycerophospholipid composition and spatial distribution were analyzed by targeted lipidomics and AFADESI-QQQ-MSI-based spatial metabolomics. Lands cycle enzyme expression was measured by RT-qPCR and western blotting. RESULTS: DCX dose-dependently reduced infarct volume and attenuated neuronal damage, accompanied by decreased ROS and MDA, elevated GSH, and preserved mitochondrial membrane integrity. Lipidomic analysis revealed that DCX shifted phospholipids from peroxidation-prone PUFA-PLs to oxidation-resistant SFA/MUFA-PLs in a spatially specific manner, reducing PUFA-PLs from 90.7% to 82.9% and increasing SFA/MUFA-PLs from 9.3% to 17.1%. SFA-PLs were region-selectively restored in hippocampus and thalamus, and MUFA-PLs in the corpus callosum and internal capsule. Mechanistically, DCX concurrently upregulated PLA2G6, ACSL3, MBOAT2, and LPCAT1, consistent with Lands cycle-mediated deacylation and reacylation. Five brain-penetrating constituents (senkyunolide A, butylphthalide, levistilide A, ferulic acid, and gastrodin) modulated these enzymes in vitro. CONCLUSION: This work provides the first evidence that DCX elicits spatially specific phospholipid remodeling toward oxidation-resistant species, an effect associated with Lands cycle activation and its brain-penetrating constituents. This remodeling may reduce peroxidation substrate availability and counteract lipid peroxidation in cerebral ischemia.

articles.title: Early PEG-bHb resuscitation for hemorrhagic shock: Attenuation of acute kidney injury via the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hemorrhagic shock (HS) is a major cause of traumatic death, strongly influenced by resuscitation timing. This study explored the protective effects and mechanisms of early polyethylene glycol-conjugated bovine hemoglobin (PEG-bHb) resuscitation in HS treatment. METHODS: Following subjecting HS, rats received PEG-bHb resuscitation at 0-30 min (R_30), 30-60 min (R_60), or 60-90 min (R_90), or conventional crystalloid-colloid solution as control. Hemodynamic, acid-base, and microcirculatory parameters, survival time, renal histopathology, and pimonidazole hypoxia staining were assessed to verify the resuscitation effect. Renal transcriptomic profiling was performed, followed by validation of inflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, mitochondrial morphology, and Nrf2/HO-1 pathway activation. The Nrf2 inhibitor ML385 was used to confirm pathway involvement. RESULTS: All PEG-bHb groups showed restoration of hemodynamic, acid-base, and microcirculatory parameters, yet R_30 and R_60 significantly prolonged survival (27.59 h, 28.03 h) versus HES (<4 h). Histopathological and pimonidazole hypoxia staining showed markedly attenuated renal injury and reduced renal tissue hypoxia after early resuscitation. Transcriptomic and validation results revealed that R_30 suppressed renal inflammation, oxidative stress, and apoptosis, restored mitochondrial morphology, and activated the Nrf2/HO-1 pathway. Nrf2 inhibition by ML385 abolished these protective effects. CONCLUSIONS: Early PEG-bHb resuscitation ameliorates HS-induced acute kidney injury and improves survival by activating the Nrf2/HO-1 signaling pathway.

articles.title: Bergenin attenuates diabetic cardiomyopathy by inhibiting oxidative stress and ferroptosis through modulation of the YAP signaling axis.
articles.abstract: AIMS: Diabetes mellitus-associated cardiac dysfunction arises from metabolic imbalance, oxidative stress, inflammation, maladaptive remodeling, and impaired cardiac performance. Bergenin (BER), a naturally occurring small molecule with antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and metabolic regulatory properties, has shown therapeutic potential; however, its role in diabetic cardiomyopathy (DCM) remains unclear. This study investigated the cardioprotective effects of BER in DCM, with particular emphasis on oxidative stress, the Hippo-Yes-associated protein (YAP), and ferroptosis signaling axis. MATERIALS AND METHODS: DCM was induced in rats using a high-fat diet combined with low-dose streptozotocin (STZ). Diabetic rats received BER (25 or 50 mg/kg/day) or empagliflozin (10 mg/kg/day). Cardiac function was evaluated by echocardiography, followed by histopathological and molecular analyses. To further investigate the underlying mechanisms, H9c2 cardiomyoblasts exposed to high glucose were used for in vitro assessment of oxidative stress, Hippo-YAP signaling, and ferroptosis-related markers. KEY FINDINGS: In vivo, BER treatment significantly improved cardiac function, attenuated histopathological injury, and reduced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and fibrosis in diabetic rats. Consistent with these findings, in vitro, BER reduced reactive oxygen species generation, restored mitochondrial integrity, and prevented high glucose-induced injury in H9c2 cells. Mechanistically, BER modulated YAP signaling and suppressed ferroptosis-related changes. YAP silencing attenuated the protective effects of BER, supporting a critical role for YAP in mediating its anti-ferroptotic effects. SIGNIFICANCE: These findings demonstrate that BER exerts cardioprotective effects against diabetes-associated cardiac dysfunction and provide mechanistic evidence implicating the YAP-ferroptosis axis in this protection. Further studies are warranted to establish its translational potential.

articles.title: Artesunate targets STAT3 to alleviate Hodgkin's lymphoma via JAK-STAT/PD-L1 axis.
articles.abstract: Relapsed or refractory Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) is resistant to existing chemotherapy and PD-1 inhibitors, creating an urgent need for safe and effective drugs with novel mechanisms of action. Artesunate (ART), a classic antimalarial agent, has recently demonstrated broad-spectrum antitumor activity. However, its direct targets and core molecular mechanisms in HL remain unclear. In this study, we combined HuProt™ 20 K human proteome microarray, network pharmacology, molecular docking, and in vitro functional assays to identify the key targets and signaling pathways of ART against HL. Critical functional residues were validated through site-directed mutagenesis. Proteome microarray and protein-protein interaction network analysis identified STAT3 as the core target of ART in HL. Molecular docking revealed a binding energy of -7.2 kcal/mol between ART and STAT3, with Glu638 identified as a critical interacting residue. Functional experiments confirmed that ART significantly inhibited STAT3 phosphorylation, reduced the levels of soluble PD-L1, BCL-XL, and IL-6 in the supernatant, and suppressed HL cell proliferation and migration. Notably, both the STAT3E638A mutation and STAT3-siRNA completely abolished the antitumor effects of ART. Collectively, ART blocks the JAK-STAT/PD-L1 signaling axis by targeting Glu638 of STAT3, achieving dual effects of inhibiting tumor survival and reversing immune evasion. This work identifies STAT3 as a direct binding target of ART in HL and establishes Glu638 as a critical functional site, providing a robust theoretical and experimental foundation for repurposing ART in the treatment of relapsed or refractory HL.

articles.title: Influence of dietary protein deficiency on the progression and resolution of CCl₄-induced liver damage.
articles.abstract: Malnutrition remains a major global health challenge and is associated with increased susceptibility to liver disease and impaired recovery following hepatic injury. This research assesses the impact of a low-protein diet (LPD) on mice subjected to carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄)-induced liver damage. How an established state of protein deficiency affects the temporal progression of liver injury and the subsequent process of hepatic recovery remains poorly understood. Therefore, this study investigated the influence of long-term dietary protein-deficiency on the progression and resolution of CCl₄-induced liver injury using a longitudinal experimental approach. A preliminary dose-selection study identified 2 mL/kg CCl₄ as the optimal dose in both dietary groups-normal diet (ND) and LPD. The time course of injury due to CCl₄ post-administration was assessed at 0-72 h. Injury was apparent by 1 h, reached a maximum at 24 h, and was more significant in the LPD group compared to the ND group. By 72 h, ND mice showed near-complete recovery, whereas liver injury persisted in LPD mice. Inflammatory markers (TNF-α and IL-6) indicated greater inflammatory responses in the LPD mice. Also, elevated PCNA and MDA levels in the LPD mice suggest that there was increased oxidative stress in addition to an increased compensatory cell proliferation response. Histopathological assessment revealed more extensive tissue damage, including necrosis, apoptosis, and delayed regenerative recovery, in LPD mice. Therefore, by defining the temporal pattern of liver injury and recovery, this study provides a framework for identifying optimal intervention windows and evaluating therapeutic strategies under protein-deficiency conditions.

articles.title: Albumin/BSH-fused nanoparticle for boron neutron capture therapy of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.
articles.abstract: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) is a highly aggressive malignant tumor which suffers from poor prognosis and limited therapeutic remedies. As a physiologically-oriented radiotherapy and highly tumor-specific modality, boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) shows great potential for the treatment of ESCC. Since efficacy of BNCT is critically restricted to boron drugs, novel boron agents with satisfactory boron load and intracellular uptake are highly demanded. Herein, we developed a novel albumin/BSH-conjugated nanoparticle (BSH@Alb) as a safe and effective boron agent. It resulted BSH@Alb displayed uniform particle size, high encapsulation efficiency (93.1 ± 0.39%), loading capacity (15.52 ± 0.41%) and good stability in different solution (water, PBS and plasma). Collectively, BSH@Alb significantly enhanced intracellular boron accumulation and showed acceptable cytocompatibility in comparison with prototype BSH, supporting its potential value for BNCT therapy as a promising boron-delivery candidate.

articles.title: Nicotinate Phosphoribosyltransferase controls aggressiveness, Ca2+ homeostasis, and NAD+-derived Ca2+ mobilizing second messengers in triple-negative breast cancer.
articles.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) represents the most aggressive form of breast cancer (BC), being characterized by a high metastatic rate and a poor prognosis due to its tendency to relapse and the lack of targeted therapies. Inhibition of NAD+ synthesis, mostly by targeting Nicotinamide Phosphoribosyltransferase in the salvage pathway, showed promise as anticancer therapy, as NAD+ is implicated in tumor growth, energy production, motion and invasiveness, immune response, and multi-drug resistance. We investigated the role of Nicotinate Phosphoribosyltransferase (NAPRT), the rate-limiting enzyme for NAD+ synthesis starting from nicotinate, in TNBC proliferation, invasiveness, also through the use of a 3D culture model, and in Ca2+ homeostasis. Our results demonstrated that NAPRT promotes tumor aggression and determines the concomitant increase of the cytosolic Ca2+ levels and the decrease in state of replenishment of Thapsigargin-sensitive ER Ca2+ stores. Also, NAPRT overexpression increased the levels of the Ca2+-mobilizing messengers cyclic ADPR and Nicotinic Acid Adenine Dinucleotide Phosphate (measurements with a newly developed assay) and the pharmacological CD38 or SARM1 inhibition reverted the NAPRT-induced changes in Ca2+ homeostasis. Therefore, targeting NAPRT may represent a promising strategy to slow down TNBC growth and progression.

articles.title: Preventing oxaliplatin-induced peripheral neuropathy with a Pt(IV)-Mn(II) prodrug: Toxicity, behavioral and X-ray fluorescence microscopy studies.
articles.abstract: Although widely used in chemotherapeutic treatments, platinum (Pt)-based drugs -namely cisplatin (Cis), oxaliplatin (Ox), and carboplatin- encounter several drawbacks that significantly limit their clinically applicable doses, such as the development of various side effects. These toxicities, including nephrotoxicity and neurotoxicity associated with Cis and Ox, respectively, arise from the lack of selectivity of these drugs toward cancer cells. While numerous alternative treatments -some employing a Pt(IV) prodrug strategy- have been investigated in preclinical settings for their anticancer activity, studies evaluating their systemic toxicities remain scarce. However, assessing these toxicities is crucial for the development of improved therapies. This study aimed to evaluate the systemic toxicities induced by PtC5Mn, a novel Pt(IV)-Mn(II) prodrug reported to exhibit anticancer activity in both in vitro and in vivo models of colorectal cancer, as well as Mn1C5, its corresponding Mn(II) complex that mimics superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity, in combination with Ox. Additionally, their potential protective effects against Ox-induced peripheral neuropathy were explored through behavioral studies and mapping of Pt localization in sciatic nerves sections by Synchrotron-based Scanning X-Ray Fluorescence microscopy. Our results support the use of Pt(IV) prodrugs and redox modulation by SOD mimics for the mitigation of oxaliplatin-associated off-target effects.

articles.title: Jiedu Quyu Ziyin Decoction attenuates high-phosphate-induced calcification-associated phenotypes in cultured human aortic smooth muscle cells.
articles.abstract: Vascular calcification is one of the complications related to chronic kidney disease, and there are correlations between vascular calcification and oxidative stress, inflammation, and ferroptosis. This study examined whether Jiedu Quyu Ziyin Decoction (JQZYD) attenuates high-phosphate-induced calcification in cultured human aortic smooth muscle cells and evaluated the contribution of NRF2-associated antioxidant signalling. Human aortic vascular smooth muscle cells were exposed to high-phosphate conditions and treated with JQZYD. Calcification was assessed by Alizarin Red S staining, calcium content, alkaline phosphatase activity, and osteogenic markers. Ferroptosis-associated changes were evaluated by BODIPY 581/591 C11 oxidation, intracellular Fe2⁺, glutathione, glutathione peroxidase activity, and GPX4/SLC7A11 expression. NRF2 activation was assessed by immunofluorescence and protein analysis. Ferrostatin-1, RSL3, and NFE2L2 silencing were used for mechanistic evaluation. Inflammatory mediators and conditioned-medium effects were also examined. JQZYD reduced high-phosphate-induced mineral deposition, osteogenic marker expression, lipid peroxidation, Fe2⁺ accumulation, and inflammatory responses. These changes were accompanied by increased glutathione peroxidase activity, greater NRF2 nuclear accumulation, higher GPX4 and SLC7A11 transcript abundance, and increased NRF2 and GPX4 protein abundance. Ferrostatin-1 reproduced several protective effects of JQZYD. RSL3 and NFE2L2 silencing partially attenuated JQZYD-associated protection, supporting contributions of GPX4-related lipid peroxide regulation and NRF2-associated signalling without establishing direct NRF2 regulation of SLC7A11/GPX4 or pathway order. Conditioned medium from JQZYD-treated donor cells induced weaker inflammatory and calcific responses in recipient HASMCs, although the responsible mediators and potential contribution of residual treatment components remained unresolved. JQZYD attenuated high-phosphate-induced calcification-associated phenotypes and accompanying oxidative and inflammatory responses in cultured HASMCs. NFE2L2 silencing supports NRF2 involvement without establishing direct regulation of SLC7A11/GPX4 or pathway order. These findings are restricted to a cellular model and do not establish prevention of vascular calcification or therapeutic efficacy in CKD. Validation in CKD-relevant animal models and more physiologically complex vascular systems is required.

articles.title: Desethylhydroxychloroquine and CYP2D6 polymorphisms are associated with low disease activity in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.
articles.abstract: AIMS: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is standard therapy for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), but the clinical relevance of its active metabolite, desethylhydroxychloroquine (DHCQ), remains unclear. We examined whether DHCQ exposure is more closely related to disease control than HCQ exposure in Japanese patients with SLE. METHODS: Patients receiving HCQ for at least 6 months were enrolled. Whole-blood and plasma HCQ and DHCQ, and plasma 4β-hydroxycholesterol (a CYP3A activity marker), were measured by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS), and CYP2D6 (*2, *5, *10) and CYP3A5 (*3) were genotyped. The primary outcome was low disease activity (LDA), defined as SLEDAI-2K ≤ 4 with oral corticosteroids ≤5 mg/day. Exposures were analysed as continuous variables (log-transformed, per 1 SD) in multivariable logistic regression; cutoff-based analyses were exploratory, with optimism assessed by bootstrap resampling. RESULTS: Among 102 patients, 36 (35.3%) attained LDA. The 23 (22.5%) CYP2D6 intermediate metabolisers had lower DHCQ/HCQ ratios and weight-adjusted DHCQ concentration-to-dose ratios than normal metabolisers in both matrices. HCQ concentrations and CYP genotypes were not associated with LDA. Adjusted odds ratios per 1 SD increase were 1.80 (95% CI 1.10-2.95) for plasma DHCQ, 2.10 (1.23-3.59) for the plasma DHCQ/HCQ ratio, 1.73 (1.04-2.88) for whole-blood DHCQ and 2.36 (1.32-4.23) for the whole-blood DHCQ/HCQ ratio. Discrimination was modest (AUC 0.62-0.67; lower bootstrap limits 0.50-0.56). CONCLUSIONS: CYP2D6 genotype was the principal determinant of DHCQ exposure. Higher DHCQ concentrations and DHCQ/HCQ ratios, but not HCQ concentrations or genotypes, were associated with LDA, supporting DHCQ as a candidate exposure marker requiring prospective validation.

articles.title: Availability and reimbursement of fixed-dose combination medicines for hypertension treatment in Central and Eastern Europe.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) represent an important strategy in modern pharmacotherapy and are particularly beneficial in the treatment of chronic conditions such as hypertension because they reduce pill burden and may improve patient adherence to therapy. OBJECTIVES: The primary objective of this study was to compare reimbursement, pricing, and availability policies for FDC medicines used in the treatment of arterial hypertension across 15 CEE countries. Additionally, the study aimed to assess differences in HTA requirements and patient co-payments among the analyzed countries. METHODS: Data were collected from the reimbursement systems of 15 CEE countries using a questionnaire distributed to native experts in each country to ensure contextual accuracy. The list of potential active substance combinations was derived from established clinical guidelines. Associations were assessed using Spearman's rank correlation coefficients and generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs). RESULTS: Substantial variation in reimbursement requirements was observed across CEE countries. The greatest variability concerned the inclusion of adherence and persistence outcomes in reimbursement decision-making processes. Seven countries considered these aspects in their reimbursement assessments, whereas the remaining countries did not. The four most frequently reimbursed two-component FDCs were combinations of ARBs with CCBs, ACEIs with CCBs, ACEIs with diuretics, and ARBs with diuretics. Public pharmaceutical expenditure related to hypertension treatment varied substantially across countries; with Estonia allocating the highest proportion of hypertension reimbursement expenditure to FDCs (68% in 2022). The time required for inclusion on reimbursement lists also differed markedly, ranging from less than 3 months in Latvia and Lithuania to more than 12 months in Albania and Romania. Spearman correlation analyses demonstrated that the total number of reimbursed FDCs in a given country was significantly associated with HTA requirements for FDCs containing previously reimbursed components (ρ = 0.641, p = 0.011) and with the time from reimbursement application to inclusion on the reimbursement list (ρ = -0.548, p = 0.041). Multivariable GLMM analysis confirmed that: i) countries with less stringent requirements for FDCs containing already reimbursed components (i.e., countries that either do not require an HTA assessment or make the HTA requirement contingent on the manufacturer's proposed price) had a significantly higher number of reimbursed FDCs (p = 0.001); and ii) countries with less stringent HTA requirements for FDCs (i.e., those that do not require additional comparators beyond the individual FDC components) also tended to have a higher number of reimbursed FDCs (p = 0.010). CONCLUSION: Across CEE countries, less burdensome HTA and reimbursement requirements for FDCs composed of already known and reimbursed active substances were associated with broader reimbursement of single-pill antihypertensive therapies. Streamlining assessment pathways for well-justified, guideline-supported combinations could improve patient access and better align reimbursement practice with current clinical guidelines, while preserving evidence-based decision-making. Common EU-level clinical assessment processes may further support consistency across national HTA systems, although pricing and reimbursement decisions remain within national competence.

articles.title: Gypenoside LI modulates autophagy-associated apoptosis in clear cell renal cell carcinoma by PPARG/PTEN/PI3K/AKT/mTOR/ULK1 signaling network.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study was conducted to comprehensively evaluate the anti-clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) activity of gypenoside LI (Gyp LI) through in vitro and in vivo models; elucidate the specific molecular pathways mediating the induction of apoptosis and autophagy in Gyp LI-treated ccRCC cells, focusing on the regulatory role of Gypenoside LI in upregulating PPARG and coordinately modulating the PTEN/PI3K/AKT/mTOR-ULK1 signaling network; and render experimental evidence and theoretical support to develop Gyp LI as a novel anti-ccRCC agent. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Human ccRCC cell lines (769-P and ACHN) and a BALB/c nude mouse xenograft model were used for this study. The suppressive effect of Gyp LI on ccRCC cell proliferation was assessed by colony formation assay, Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay, wound healing assay, and Hoechst staining. Autophagy-related ultrastructural changes in treated cells were observed by transmission electron microscopy. Western blot and quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR) were conducted to evaluate fluctuations in the expression levels of autophagic and apoptotic process markers. Putative therapeutic targets associated with Gyp LI were predicted utilizing a network pharmacology framework. Concurrently, the transcriptional control exerted by PPARG over the PTEN gene was validated by dual-luciferase reporter systems and chromatin immunoprecipitation combined with quantitative PCR. To clarify the regulatory relationships within the signaling pathway, we performed in vitro rescue experiments using target gene knockdown. Additionally, a subcutaneous xenograft model in nude mice was established for assessing the in vivo antitumor activity and biosafety of Gyp LI. Apoptosis-, autophagy-, and pathway-related protein expression in tumor tissues was assessed by Western blotting (WB) assay. RESULTS: CCK-8 reagent-based cell viability assay revealed that Gyp LI dose-dependently inhibited 769-P and ACHN cell growth, with 24-h IC50 values of 62.57 and 79.30 μM, respectively. Colony formation, wound healing, and Hoechst staining assay results collectively showed that Gyp LI suppressed cell proliferation and migration and exerted apoptotic effects. Morphological and molecular assays showed that Gyp LI-treated ccRCC cells exhibited prominent autophagosomes and autolysosomes, with upregulation of the autophagy-related proteins Beclin1, ATG5, and LC3 I/II and downregulation of P62. The antiapoptotic factor Bcl-2 exhibited substantially reduced expression, while the proapoptotic mediators caspase-3 and Bax were upregulated, these findings indicated concurrent autophagy-related alterations and apoptosis in Gyp LI-treated ccRCC cells. WB and RT-qPCR assays revealed that Gyp LI upregulated the mRNA and protein expression of the transcription factor PPARG.
